What Are We Living For? Finding the Door for the Key

He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet so that man can’t find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end. (Ecclesiastes 3:11)
Brothers and sisters, peace! Let me ask you the question that should be asked least on a Monday morning: when the alarm goes off, why do you get up?

You might say, to go to work. Why go to work? To earn money. Why earn money? To pay the mortgage and cover the kids’ cram school. Why does the child go to cram school? So he can find a good job later. What is a good job for? To earn money to pay the mortgage and then pay for his own children’s cram school. Friends, by the fifth layer of this question, most people say, “Pastor, please stop asking, I have a train to catch.”

Today we are going to keep asking down to the sixth layer. And let me say first: asking this question does not mean your faith is weak. There is a whole book in the Bible that is the record of one man asking down to the sixth layer.
“Vanity of vanities,” says the Preacher; “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.” What does man gain from all his labor in which he labors under the sun? (Ecclesiastes 1:2-3)
The little scrap of paper in the camp

In 1945, in a subcamp of a concentration camp in southern Germany, there was a Viennese doctor named Frankl. In his hand were small scraps of paper he had gotten from the camp office, and from memory he was rewriting the manuscript that had been taken from him. He was Jewish. In 1942 he was taken away with his family; his father died in Theresienstadt, his mother and brother died in Auschwitz, and his wife never came back either.

After the war he returned to Vienna, and in 1946 he spent only nine days dictating a book. The English edition is the famous Man’s Search for Meaning. In it he quoted a line from Nietzsche, roughly: a person who knows why he lives can bear almost any how. He saw that those in the camp who managed to hold on were often people who still had one thing left undone, or someone in their heart who was waiting for them.

Please notice that he did not say that those who survived were people of meaning and those who died lacked it. He knew very well that surviving there involved a great deal of luck. What he meant was that besides food, a person needs a “why.”
The sponge that wiped away the horizon

The second answer is colder. In 1882 Nietzsche wrote a parable in which a madman ran into the marketplace and cried out: who gave us the sponge to wipe away the entire horizon? Nietzsche was not throwing a victory party. He was warning the Europe of his day: you think that removing God just means one less program on Sunday, but you have removed up and down and left and right along with it.

By 1942 the French writer Camus, in The Myth of Sisyphus, began by calling whether life is worth living the one truly serious philosophical problem. His claim was that people crave meaning while the world stays silent, and that is the absurd. So what do we do? His answer was not to give up, to live with clear eyes, to push that stone and keep on revolting.

Brothers and sisters, here I want to pause and say a few words to someone who may be listening. If lately the thought “I don’t want to live anymore” keeps coming up in your heart, thank you for still sitting here today, or still listening. This thought does not mean you are weak, and it does not mean you have no faith. It means you are very tired. Please tell someone you trust today. In Taiwan you can call the Peace of Mind Hotline 1925, or Lifeline 1995, and if you cannot get through, call again. Elsewhere, please find your local crisis line; if there is immediate danger, call the emergency number or go to the emergency room. You are also welcome to come and find us right after the service. You deserve to be accompanied well.

The third answer is one that many friends who do not yet believe will give today: I don’t believe in God, but I live a very meaningful life. I love my family, I rescue stray animals, I volunteer. Brothers and sisters, please don’t rush to argue with him. What he says is true.

The American philosopher Susan Wolf argues that when what you are genuinely engaged in is also truly worthwhile in itself, meaning arises. Her discussion deliberately does not presuppose God. A 2021 Pew Research Center survey of 17 advanced economies found that in 14 of them the most commonly mentioned source of meaning was family; Taiwan is a little different, where the most commonly mentioned was society, including convenient living, national health insurance and freedom. Not many people think first of God. That is the world we live in.

So here is a question worth thinking about together: family is good, health insurance is good, and both deserve our thanks. But family members will leave, bodies will age, and society will change. While all of these are in place, we live very well; when they begin to loosen, will my “why” still hold?
The spiritual meaning: be honest first, then answer

What moves me most about Ecclesiastes is that it lets a person finish speaking his despair. The Teacher even wrote words like “so I hated life.” That sentence was not edited out; it stayed in the canon. God’s word has this much room, and our churches should too. The next time someone tells you, “I don’t know what I’m living for,” please don’t rush to quote a verse. First pull up a chair and sit down.
A hundred uses for a key

Let me give you an illustration. You find an old key in a drawer, beautifully shaped. You can use it as a bookmark, as a letter opener, or hang it on your backpack as a charm, and your friends even praise your taste. None of these uses is wrong, and you can enjoy them very much.
But if this key was originally the key to a particular door, then sooner or later, on some evening, you will pick it up and think: what does this actually open?

That is the problem with life. Is my whole life a piece of metal for me to use as I please, or is there a door it was made to open? If it is the former, whatever you do with it counts, and no one can say you used it wrongly. If it is the latter, then no matter how brilliantly you use it, a space will remain empty in your heart.

Ecclesiastes puts that empty space in another sentence: God “has also set eternity in their hearts.” Think about it, everyone: a cat does not sit under the sunset pondering its cat life. A human being does. A lifespan of a hundred years carrying a heart that wants forever. That this size does not fit is a feeling we all share.

The psychologists Shigehiro Oishi and Ed Diener analyzed Gallup data from 132 countries and more than 140,000 people, and the result is interesting: people in wealthier countries are more satisfied with life but rate their lives as less meaningful, while in poorer countries it is the opposite. They suggested that the strength of religious belief may be one of the key factors.

Brothers and sisters, I want to speak about this study very carefully. It is a country-level correlation. It does not mean that having money makes you empty, and it certainly does not mean poverty is lovely; we must never use it to comfort someone who is hungry. It only reminds us of one thing: air conditioning and meaning are two different things.

I also have to say honestly that none of this proves God. Nagel, a philosopher who does not believe in God, says the sense of absurdity is just a conflict within a person: we take life seriously and yet can step back and doubt it, and there is no need to despair over this. That is a very serious answer. What we Christians want to say is this: the longing deserves to be taken seriously, and it may be pointing to a door.
The spiritual meaning: your existence has an object

For by him all things were created in the heavens and on the earth, visible things and invisible things, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers. All things have been created through him and for him. (Colossians 1:16)

Notice the last words: for Him. The “Him” Paul speaks of is Christ. So the Bible’s answer to “what am I living for” is not a concept, nor a set of success principles, but a person. The door has a name.

Someone asked Jesus: which commandment is the greatest? He did not hand out a list of thirty. He said to love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul and mind, and next, to love your neighbor as yourself. The first question of the Westminster Shorter Catechism of 1647 answers the same way: the chief end of man is to glorify God and to enjoy Him forever. Did you hear that, everyone? “Enjoy Him.” The purpose God has placed in your life has joy inside it.
3. The One who walked into the emptiness
Under the sun, and above the sun
But at this point someone may say in his heart: Pastor, I know all about loving God and loving others, but I can’t do it. I have always lived for myself, and I am tired.

This is exactly where the gospel begins. That Lord does not stand at the door holding an exam paper and waiting for you. He Himself walked into “under the sun.” He too labored, wept, was betrayed by a friend, and cried out on the cross the deepest cry in the Psalms. He died for our sins and on the third day rose from the dead.
He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again. (2 Corinthians 5:15)
The Teacher kept asking: under the sun, what profit is there? Paul answers him in the chapter on the resurrection.
Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, because you know that your labor is not in vain in the Lord. (1 Corinthians 15:58)

Not in vain. You accompany your child to the doctor in the middle of the night and no one sees; you care for a parent with dementia who no longer recognizes you; you have prayed for someone for twenty years and he still has not turned back. If under the sun is all there is, these things may be forgotten. But Jesus rose, so all this love has somewhere to go.
The spiritual meaning: from self-centered to selfless

We in 321 often speak of being self-centered and being selfless. A self-centered life is one where I am the lead, even God is my supporting actor, and my career, my name and my plans all need God to bless them. The problem is that the lead grows old, and the stage gets torn down.

Selflessness does not mean wiping yourself out, nor does it mean you are unimportant. God called you by name, so of course you matter. Being selfless means giving the lead role back to Jesus: let Jesus reign, let Jesus receive all the glory. The wonderful thing is that when the key goes into its door, it is not diminished at all; for the first time it becomes itself.

So back to the Monday morning alarm. Tomorrow it will still ring, the mortgage will still need paying, the kids will still go to cram school. Believing in Jesus does not make these things disappear. What changes is the answer at the sixth layer: I live because there is a Lord who made me, who loves me and gave Himself for me, and today I will carry His love to everyone I meet.

This week, please do one small thing: write a “living declaration” beginning with “I live for…” and keep it in your phone’s notes. A week later, look back and see how much of it actually appeared in your calendar. It doesn’t matter if it is not beautifully written; God values what is real.

Lord Jesus, who created me and gave Your life for me, I confess that I often cover the emptiness in my heart with busyness. Thank You for not rebuking me because I asked, “What am I living for?” Be my reason for living Yourself, lead me to love You with all my heart and to love the people around me. If anyone is so tired right now that he does not want to walk any further, draw near to him and send someone to accompany him, so that he has the courage to ask for help today. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Yahweh is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit. (Psalm 34:18)
Brothers and sisters, the best thing Job’s three friends ever did was to say nothing for seven whole days.
So they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great. (Job 2:13)

They did those seven days so well. They came a long way, and when they saw Job from a distance they did not recognize him, so they wept aloud, tore their robes, and sat down on the ground. They had not prepared a script, and they did not bring a single “actually, God is trying to teach you.”
Then on the eighth day they opened their mouths. Friends, this is where the disaster begins.

Today’s topic is the heaviest lesson in the whole Life’s Questions Hall, so I want to say first how this sermon will go. I do not plan to solve the problem of suffering today. I cannot solve it, and people a hundred times smarter than I am have not solved it through the ages. Among us today, or listening online, there may be someone who has just lost a child, someone who has just received a medical report, someone whose home hides a hurt that no one knows about. To you I only want to say: you do not have to figure it out today. If halfway through you need to step out for air, that is all right. If you are angry with God, that is all right too.

There is one more thing I must say first. If you are thinking right now that you do not want to live, thank you for still being here today. This thought does not mean you are weak, and it does not mean you have no faith. Please tell someone you trust today, and seek professional help. In Taiwan you can call the Peace of Mind Hotline 1925, or Lifeline 1995, and if you cannot get through, call again. Elsewhere, please find your local crisis line; if there is immediate danger, call your local emergency number. After the service you are also welcome to come and find us directly.
1. Three things we should not say
First: “There must be a reason. You should reflect.”

Job’s friends spoke for more than thirty chapters, and the core was really one sentence: God is just, so if you are suffering, something must be wrong with you. The logic is so neat that you could almost turn it into a table. The Chinese world has its own versions: “Did you not worship the ancestors properly?” “Are you paying off a debt from a previous life?” The church version is more polite: “Is there some sin you haven’t confessed?”
Once Jesus’ disciples saw a man who was born blind, and they went straight into research mode, asking: who sinned? Was it the man himself, or his parents? Jesus’ answer tore up the whole table.
Jesus answered, “This man didn’t sin, nor did his parents, but that the works of God might be revealed in him. (John 9:3)

Another time people were talking about the tower in Siloam that fell and killed eighteen people. Jesus asked: do you think those people were worse offenders than everyone else? He answered it Himself: “I tell you, no.” So, brothers and sisters, the next time there is a disaster on the news, please do not rush to issue a press release on God’s behalf. Of those in the earthquake, in the car accident, on the hospital bed, no one has the right to say they deserved it.
Second: “It’s all part of God’s good plan.”

This one is the hardest to handle, because behind it stands a real verse. Romans 8:28 says, “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God.” I believe this verse, without discounting a single word. But what Paul speaks of is God’s final work; he did not say that every single event is good in itself. The same Paul, in 1 Corinthians, calls death “the last enemy.”

Let me give you an illustration. A traditional Chinese herbal prescription may contain huanglian, a very bitter herb. However good the prescription, huanglian taken alone is still bitter, and no one calls it sweet just because the prescription is good. Even less would anyone walk up to a patient who is vomiting and begin lecturing on pharmacology. Romans 8:28 is a prescription, and God is the one who writes it. Those of us standing beside the sickbed should be holding a cup of warm water.

So if you go to a funeral hall, please do not say to a mother who has lost her child, “God wanted him to go home, this is a blessing.” That sentence speaks for God words He has not spoken to her. If she herself one day gets there, she will say it herself. That is her right, not your assignment.

There is a very famous Christian philosopher named Wolterstorff, who taught at Yale. His 25-year-old son Eric died in a mountain-climbing accident. This scholar, who had spent his whole life studying philosophy and God, wrote a thin book in 1987 called Lament for a Son. In it he frankly said that he did not know why God watched his son fall. A professional Christian philosopher, simply writing, “I do not know.” Twelve years later he said that the wound was no longer so raw, but it was still there.
Everyone, if your wound is still there after ten years, nothing has gone wrong with you. That pain is often the very shape that love takes when it remains.
The spiritual meaning: God rebuked the explainers
The most astonishing part of the book of Job is its ending. Through the whole book, Job said many very impolite things to God, while his friends kept defending God. So what did God say?

It was so, that after Yahweh had spoken these words to Job, Yahweh said to Eliphaz the Temanite, “My wrath is kindled against you, and against your two friends; for you have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job has. (Job 42:7)

To the one who cried out at God, God said he had spoken somewhat rightly; to those who defended God, God was angry. That does not mean Job was right in everything; God also questioned him out of the whirlwind. But the contrast is enough to keep us alert for a lifetime. God would rather be honestly questioned by a wounded person than cheaply defended by a crowd of people who are not hurting.
2. The Bible allows you to pray like this

Many Christians think a prayer must have a beautiful ending. Please look at Psalm 88. From beginning to end it is a cry. Most other laments turn toward praise at the close, but this one does not. This is how its last line goes:
You have put lover and friend far from me, and my friends into darkness. (Psalm 88:18)

The last word in Hebrew is “darkness.” If this psalm were handed to a church pianist today, he would probably add two chords to help it end a bit more brightly. God did not add them. God placed a prayer that ends in darkness into the Bible, so that all who walk to that place would know: someone has been here before, and this kind of prayer counts as prayer.

Everyone knows C. S. Lewis, the author of Narnia, the great defender of the faith. His wife Joy died of cancer in 1960. The next year he published a little book, A Grief Observed, under a pseudonym, because what it said was so unlike the Lewis everyone knew. When he wrote about crying out to God, it was as if he ran into a door bolted from the inside. The man who wrote a classic of apologetics, The Problem of Pain, was, when it hurt him, just like us.

There is also Joni. In 1967 she was only 17 when a diving accident left her a quadriplegic; later she had stage-three breast cancer, and to this day she lives with severe chronic pain. This sister, who has served all her life, reminds us that the original meaning of the word “compassion” is “to suffer together.” Pastor Keller wrote a thick book on suffering, and when she wrote a review of it, she also said that to someone who clenches a fist and asks why, the answer itself can hurt. Keller himself later got pancreatic cancer and died in 2023 under hospice care. The man who wrote the book also walked down that road in the end.
The spiritual meaning: first learn to sit down

One psychological study surveyed people’s anger toward God and found that after negative events this feeling is not uncommon, and that if the anger drags on beyond a year without being resolved, it is most strongly linked to poorer adjustment. That is a correlation; it does not mean your anger harmed you. What I take from it is a reminder: do not keep it bottled up. Bring it to God, and bring it to someone who can sit down beside you.
Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep. (Romans 12:15)

The second half of this verse is what the church is less good at. We are very good at holding celebrations and not so good at weeping with people. And when someone is crying, please don’t hand over the tissue too quickly; sometimes that is a way of saying “you can stop now.”

All right, so where is God? I cannot tell you why it is you. I can only take you to see a few places. The first place is Bethany. Lazarus had been dead four days, and Mary came weeping. Jesus knew what He would do in a few minutes. If anyone in the world was qualified to say “don’t cry, it will be all right in a moment,” it was Him.

When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews weeping who came with her, he groaned in the spirit and was troubled, and said, “Where have you laid him?” They told him, “Lord, come and see.” Jesus wept. (John 11:33-35)
One of the shortest sentences in the whole Bible: “Jesus wept.” The One who knew the ending wept. What makes you think you are not allowed to?
He is on the hospital bed, not in the companion’s chair

The second place. Those of you who have stayed in a hospital in Taiwan know that there is a kind of bedside chair for the companion, narrow and hard, which can just about be unfolded into a bed. The person sleeping in it cannot solve anything; he cannot read the reports, and he cannot feel the pain for you. But when you wake in the middle of the night and turn your head and see someone curled up there, in that moment you know you have not been abandoned.

The Christian faith says something that goes further than this. God did not stay in the companion’s chair. He lay down on the hospital bed. On the cross Jesus cried out the first line of Psalm 22: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” He died for our sins, and He went into the deepest place of human suffering.
On the third day He rose. But please notice one detail: on His risen body, the nail marks were still there. He said to Thomas:
Then he said to Thomas, “Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing.” (John 20:27)

So when you bring Him your complaints, the One across from you is not a counselor who has never been hurt. Theologians are still discussing today how exactly God’s nature relates to suffering. It is a serious question, and the church through the ages has put it in different ways. But everyone agrees that the suffering Jesus is real, and that He is not far from those who suffer.
The spiritual meaning: a night that will end
He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more; neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain any more. The first things have passed away.” (Revelation 21:4)

Please notice that God wipes them with His own hand. He does not tell you those tears do not matter; He says that one day He will wipe them away Himself. This hope will not take away your pain today. It only tells you that the pain will not be the last word.

Brothers and sisters, in 321 we often say “Jesus is my example.” In the matter of suffering, we see that He wept first and spoke afterward. We also often say “People matter more than tasks.” A person who is suffering is not a ministry item for us; he is a person. You may not be able to help much, but you can sit down.

So this week there are two assignments. If you are suffering, please take a sheet of paper and write four lines of your own lament: “God, I…” “Why did You…” “I need…” “I still say to You…” If you cannot write the fourth line, leave it blank; Psalm 88 did not write it either. Then read it aloud to someone you trust. If you are not in suffering right now, think of someone who is, and send them one line: “I don’t know what to say, but I remember you. Can I come and sit with you for a while this week?” No Bible verse, and no advice.

If your pain comes from someone else hurting you, whether at home or in the church, it is not your fault, and no one should tell you to put up with it a little longer. In Taiwan you can call the 113 Protection Hotline. Go first to a safe place; God does not want you to stay in danger to prove your faith.

Lord Jesus, You wept at Lazarus’s tomb, and Your body bears wounds. We do not really know how to pray, so we hand You these tears and questions. Draw near to every aching heart here today, and forgive us for the times we have hurt people with beautiful words. If someone is so tired tonight that he does not want to walk any further, keep watch over him, and give him the courage to tell someone today. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

If God Is Good, Why Is There Evil?
Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good. (Romans 12:21)
Brothers and sisters, one of the strongest arguments against Christianity was written by a Christian novelist.

Dostoevsky, a Russian Orthodox believer. In The Brothers Karamazov he has the elder brother Ivan tell the devout younger brother Alyosha, one by one, stories of innocent children being tortured. When he finishes, Ivan says: even if there is to be an eternal great harmony one day, and everyone will understand, if the price of admission is the unavenged tears of a single child, then I return the ticket. Ivan makes a special point: I am not saying God does not exist, I am just refusing to accept this ticket.

Everyone, a Christian writer made his opponent’s argument this powerful. That gives us an example. If today you have a friend who does not believe in God because he has seen too much injustice, he is not less intelligent and he is not hard-hearted. He may care about that child more than we do. Today we are going to listen carefully to this question.

One more thing I must say first. Last unit we spoke about accompanying people in suffering, and that lesson was for those who are hurting. Today’s lesson is more for those who are asking. If you have just been wounded, today’s discussion may be too cold for you; please feel free to skip it at any time and go back to the previous lesson first. Arguments cannot be used as comfort.
The true origin of a famous saying

Many of you may have seen this passage: if God wants to remove evil but cannot, He is not all-powerful; if He can but will not, He is not all-good; if He both can and will, where does evil come from? On the internet it is all said to be from the ancient Greek Epicurus. When you check, you cannot find it in his surviving writings. The earliest to attribute it to him was a Christian author, Lactantius, and it became widely known later through David Hume’s Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion in 1779. I mention this because I want us to form the habit of checking. The question itself is still very serious; it does not disappear because there is a problem with its attribution.
The accountant’s first audit: the logical version

In 1955 the Australian philosopher J. L. Mackie wrote a paper arguing that the coexistence of an all-powerful, all-good God and evil is logically contradictory. It is like an auditor saying: this ledger cannot possibly balance, there must be fraud.

In 1974 Alvin Plantinga published God, Freedom, and Evil. His response was very ingenious: if there is a kind of world in which the creatures have real freedom, able to do good and also to do evil, that may be a greater good. And even the Almighty cannot do something contradictory like “force someone to freely do good,” just as He cannot draw a square circle. Please note that he did not say this is God’s actual reason. He needed only to point out one possible way of calculating, and that is enough to withdraw the charge that “the books cannot balance.”

How did it turn out? Today the academic community broadly holds that he successfully answered the logical version of that time. Mackie himself admitted in 1982 that it no longer counted as a contradiction, but he added that whether it truly solves the problem is another matter. Mackie was quite right: we must not pop the champagne.
The accountant’s second audit: the evidential version

Then in 1979 the philosopher William Rowe put forward a harder version. He said: lightning strikes a forest and it catches fire, a fawn is terribly burned and lies in pain alone for several days before it dies, and no one knows. What greater good could such suffering bring? Later discussion added real cases, such as the murder of a five-year-old child. He asked: if we cannot see a reason, then probably there really is none, and so there is probably no all-good God.

This time the auditor changed his wording: perhaps there is a way to calculate it, but I have gone through so many entries and cannot make sense of a single one; is this company really honest? Everyone, I do not plan to settle this question for you today, because to this day neither side has settled it completely.
The spiritual meaning: even the prophets asked

LORD, how long will I cry, and you will not hear? I cry out to you “Violence!” and will you not save? Why do you show me iniquity, and look at perversity? For destruction and violence are before me. There is strife, and contention rises up. (Habakkuk 1:2-3)

You see, Habakkuk came more than two thousand years before Mackie. God did not strike him off the list of prophets because of this; instead He had his question printed in the Bible. So if you have this question, you are standing in the company of the prophets.
2. Some honest responses, and their limits

The first response comes from Stephen Wykstra, who said in 1984: if such a God exists, it is no surprise that His reasons lie beyond our sight, just as a baby cannot understand why his mother carries him for a shot. Rowe’s counterattack was also beautiful. He said: during the shot a mother who loves her child stays beside him, holds him, and lets him feel her love. She does not disappear. But many who suffer are precisely the ones who cannot feel God.
Everyone, that punch lands solidly. Let us remember it for now, because we will come back to it.
A school for growth, and the people who were crushed

The second is John Hick’s soul-making view of 1966: a world without danger cannot produce courage, and if no one suffered, no one would learn compassion. Many who have walked through suffering can indeed testify to this. But critics ask: what about those who were utterly crushed? What about the children who never had time to grow up? Here the school metaphor falls short. We cannot avoid this question, and we certainly cannot say the word “growth” to parents who have lost a child.

The third comes from the Oxford theologian Marilyn McCord Adams. She said that when we face truly devastating evil, telling the person involved that “the whole world is better for it” is no answer. The problem has to be resolved within that person’s own life. She pointed especially to God’s becoming human Himself and bearing it together with people. We will get there in the next section.
The spiritual meaning: the line runs through me

There is one more thing we cannot leave out. When we talk about evil, our fingers point naturally at others: some dictator, some criminal. Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn spent years in the Soviet labor camps, and he wrote in The Gulag Archipelago that the line dividing good and evil does not pass between states, classes or parties; it passes through every human heart.

For from within, out of the hearts of men, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, sexual sins, murders, thefts, covetings, wickedness, deceit, lustful desires, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, and foolishness. All these evil things come from within and defile the man.” (Mark 7:21-23)

In 321 we speak of being self-centered. When people leave their place, want to be king themselves and grab power, that is the seed of evil. But I must especially remind you: this passage is for examining ourselves, and not for saying to a victim, “you share in it too.” A battered wife does not need to hear this passage; she needs safety. Victim and perpetrator must be kept apart.
The One who has the right to speak

Now back to Ivan and Alyosha. After Ivan finished, Alyosha answered with only one thing: there is an innocent victim in the world, He shed blood, and He has the right to speak. Dostoevsky did not write an essay to refute Ivan; he had Alyosha point to the cross.
Back to the shot. Rowe asked: where is the mother? The Christian answer is: this mother took the needle herself, and took it much harder than the child.
But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. (Isaiah 53:5)

I must say honestly that this does not answer where evil comes from, and it does not list all of God’s reasons. A friend who does not believe may fully say: that is not enough for me. I respect him. But this does change the direction of the question: we were asking, “God, do You care at all?” and the cross answers, “I care to this extent.” On the third day He rose, which means that evil has power, but it is not the final power.
A universe without judgment: who is it good news for

Many modern people do not like the word “judgment.” But please ask someone who has truly been harmed. If the universe ends with no one held accountable, who benefits most? The perpetrator. The victims in the Bible keep asking:

When he opened the fifth seal, I saw underneath the altar the souls of those who had been killed for the Word of God, and for the testimony of the Lamb which they had. They cried with a loud voice, saying, “How long, Master, the holy and true, until you judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?” (Revelation 6:9-10)

The Croatian theologian Miroslav Volf reflected on the war in his own homeland and wrote Exclusion and Embrace. He argued that people can put down the knife because they believe the final judgment is in God’s hands. In a comfortable study, people may find judgment uncivilized; in a burned village, the thinking is different.
The spiritual meaning: overcoming evil with good does not mean keeping people in violence

Therefore “If your enemy is hungry, feed him. If he is thirsty, give him a drink; for in doing so, you will heap coals of fire on his head.” Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good. (Romans 12:20-21)

This passage is beautiful, and it is also very easy to use to harm people. So I must say it clearly: “Don’t seek revenge yourselves” means no lynching and no repaying evil with evil. It does not mean not calling the police, not seeking help, not leaving. If you are being abused, your first task is safety. In Taiwan you can call the 113 Protection Hotline. If someone uses this passage to persuade you to stay in the violence, he has read it wrongly. If a church keeps the perpetrator’s secrets to save face, that is working together with evil. The first step in overcoming evil with good is often telling the truth.

Brothers and sisters, today we have not finished solving this question. If a friend who does not believe asks you, you can honestly say, “I have many things I don’t understand too.” Humility overcomes pride includes this as well: you do not need to win every conversation. You can say to him: the God I believe in did not give me an answer from far away. He came in Himself, and He will do justice.

This week, please do one concrete small act of overcoming evil with good. It could be supporting an organization that protects victims, accompanying a friend who is going through legal proceedings, or going to admit your wrong to someone you have hurt. Against a dark world these things are all very small, but the Bible says, “The light shines in the darkness.” Letting Jesus reign includes letting Him be the Judge, and then we can put down the knife in our hand and pick up the cup of water.

Righteous Lord, the evil in the world makes us angry and makes us confused. What we do not understand, please do not let us pretend to understand. Thank You that You did not stand far away; on the cross You bore it Yourself. Comfort the victims, restrain those who do evil, and search our own hearts. Lord, come quickly and do justice. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
1. For you or your friends, what is the one thing that most makes people doubt God’s goodness? Please listen to one another first, without rushing to answer.
2. Rowe asked, “where is the mother?” Is the answer of the cross enough for you? Where does it still feel insufficient?
3. If someone is told to “forgive and endure” and stays in a situation of being harmed, what should our small group and church do?
The last enemy that will be abolished is death. (1 Corinthians 15:26)
Brothers and sisters, we can take the fourth floor off the elevator buttons, but we cannot take that floor out of life.

When you walk into some hospitals or buildings, the elevator buttons read 1, 2, 3, 5, or 3A. How sensitive are we Chinese to that number? We even choose our phone numbers by it. When someone dies, we do not say “died.” We say “passed on,” “is no longer with us,” “was called home by the Lord,” “went home to heaven,” anything at all, except that word.

It is not only Chinese people. In 1974 there was a cultural anthropologist named Becker, who died of colon cancer at the age of 49. Two months after his death, his book won the Pulitzer Prize. Its title was The Denial of Death. He argued that a very large part of human civilization has been built so that we do not have to look at this one thing. He himself finished his last work as he was dying.

Today we are going to look at that floor. Ecclesiastes says, “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting.” This line would probably not be welcome on a wedding invitation. But the Bible asks us to look, because what we dare not look at governs us in the dark.

Before we begin, I have two things to say. The first is for you who have just lost someone: today’s content may be too fast for you. You do not need to look strong, and if you want to step out for a walk, go ahead. The second is even more important: if you are thinking right now that you do not want to live, please listen carefully. The hope of resurrection we are speaking of today is never a reason to leave early. Your life today is precious in God’s eyes. Please tell someone you trust today, and seek professional help. In Taiwan you can call the Peace of Mind Hotline 1925, or Lifeline 1995, and if you cannot get through, call again. Elsewhere, please find your local crisis line; if there is immediate danger, call your local emergency number.

Becker has a concept that I translate into plain language as “immortality projects.” Knowing that the body will fail, people want to build something that outlasts the body: a company, a reputation, a child who gets into National Taiwan University, a plaque on the wall, an offering named after someone. Everyone, there are quite a few of these in the church too. We should watch out that ministry itself can become an immortality project with my name carved on it. These things are not necessarily bad in themselves. But the problem is that construction projects stop, and plaques lose their paint.

Becker’s ideas later led to a line of psychological research called terror management theory. I have to be honest with you: one representative experiment was redone by seventeen laboratories in 2022 and did not produce the original effect. So we should not state the details too strongly. But that people fear death needs no laboratory; you know it when you receive a test report in the middle of the night.

When Zilu asked Confucius about death, he said, not yet understanding life, how can you understand death? Do well the business of living first. It is very practical wisdom. The ancient Greek Epicurus put it even more directly: while we are here, death is not; when death comes, we are not. So there is no need to be afraid. On the tombstones of some of his followers there was even something like “I am no more, and I do not mind.” Many friends who do not yet believe face death with exactly this calm today, and we should respect them.

But Epicurus’s comfort leaves one thing uncovered: he dealt only with whether “I” am afraid, and not with “you.” I am not afraid of my own disappearing, but what about my children? My wife? What hurts is often someone else’s death.
The spiritual meaning: the Bible does not prettify death
You might think Christianity says death is lovely. It does not. Paul calls it an enemy outright.
The last enemy that will be abolished is death. (1 Corinthians 15:26)

This sentence gives Christians great freedom. Death is not “a natural part of life to be accepted with a smile.” You may hate it. If you weep at the funeral until you cannot stand, no one has the right to say to you, “Your faith is weak; he went home to heaven, you should be glad.” Everyone, if you have ever said this to a grieving family, please do not say it again. Jesus knew that Lazarus was about to rise, and He still wept. Facing His own death in Gethsemane, He said to His disciples, “My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death.”
The staircase that spread too far

You have all heard of the five stages: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance. I often hear brothers and sisters say, “I should be at stage four by now, so why am I angry again?” Everyone, that staircase has harmed quite a few people.

It comes from Kübler-Ross’s book of 1969, and she was speaking of terminally ill patients, not the bereaved. She herself said that patients often have two or three of these states at the same time, and not necessarily in order. In 2017 researchers including Stroebe reviewed the evidence and argued that the theory has insufficient empirical basis, and that using it to make demands on people may even hurt them.

Closer to the research is the dual process model, and I will explain it with a picture. A bereaved person is like someone living in a house with two rooms. One is his room; you walk in, smell his clothes, and weep aloud. The other is the kitchen, where the children need to eat, the bills need to be paid, and the insurance needs to be handled. Today in the kitchen you actually laughed a little, and then the guilt came. Tomorrow you walk back into that room.

Brothers and sisters, there is nothing wrong with walking back and forth. Being in the kitchen does not mean you do not love him; going back to that room does not mean you lack faith. And no one has set a rule for how long you should stay anywhere.

But some people stay stuck for a long time and, after a long while, still cannot function normally. Psychiatry now calls this prolonged grief disorder; it was formally listed in the diagnostic manual in 2022, and a meta-analysis estimated that about ten percent of bereaved adults experience it. If this is you, it is not that your faith is not enough; it can be treated, so please go and find professional help. And if your loved one died by suicide, please do not carry alone the “I should have” thoughts. Please also do not accept words like “he must be in hell.” A person’s eternity is in God’s hands; He is more merciful than we are, and more just. He knows all of that person’s final pain.
The spiritual meaning: tears with hope

But we don’t want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who have fallen asleep, so that you don’t grieve like the rest, who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus. (1 Thessalonians 4:13-14)
Look carefully: Paul does not say do not grieve; he says do not grieve like those who have no hope. A Christian’s tears are tears with hope, and they are still tears.
3. He broke it from the inside
Near-death stories are unreliable, so what is reliable

By this point someone must be asking: Pastor, what about those stories of people who went to heaven and came back? We have to be very careful. Dr. Parnia’s AWARE study collected over two thousand cases of cardiac arrest in 2014. Among the 140 survivors who actually completed interviews, nine percent met the criteria for a near-death experience, and only one case could be partly verified. In the second-phase study in 2023, none of the 28 interviewees recognized the images placed in the experiment. The phenomenon is worth studying, but it cannot prove heaven.

What is even more embarrassing is that a best-selling Christian book, The Boy Who Came Back from Heaven, was pulled by the publisher in 2015 after the person at its center publicly said that he had not died and had not gone to heaven, and that he had been lying. Brothers and sisters, our hope does not need stories like that. A book can be pulled from the shelves, but an empty tomb cannot be pulled.
The first mango to turn yellow
But now Christ has been raised from the dead. He became the first fruit of those who are asleep. (1 Corinthians 15:20)

Those of you who have been to Yujing, the mango-growing district in Tainan, know that while the whole mango tree is still green, one always turns yellow first. When the grower sees that one, he does not say, “What a miracle, how special this one is.” He says, “This tree is about to ripen.” That is what Paul means. Jesus’ resurrection is not an exception. It is the beginning of the whole tree.

Hebrews says that He Himself partook of flesh and blood, that through death He might bring to nothing him who had the power of death, and “might deliver all of them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage.” God did not drop down a death-removal certificate from heaven. He went in, died, and broke the door from the inside.
Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies. Whoever lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?” (John 11:25-26)
Martha had been discussing doctrine with Him, and He turned the subject to Himself: “I am the resurrection and the life.” Then He asked her, and asks you: “Do you believe this?”
The spiritual meaning: how we die teaches us how to live

Church history has many testimonies like this. In April 1945, shortly before he was executed in a Nazi concentration camp, Bonhoeffer, as reported by his fellow prisoner, the British officer Payne Best, asked that a message be passed on: that this was the end, but for him the beginning of life. There is also Saunders, a doctor who began as a Christian nurse and who founded the modern hospice in London in 1967. She saw that the dying have “total pain” that is physical, emotional, social and spiritual, and she opened it to people of every faith and of none. Christians believe in resurrection, so they are willing to stay beside the dying and not look away. Many people around the world today can walk the last stretch of life with dignity, and we have her to thank as well.

So, brothers and sisters, in 321 we speak of moving from a temporary, earthly view to an eternal, God’s-eye view. This view will not make you want to leave this world; it makes you love more seriously today. Paul says:
For if we live, we live to the Lord. Or if we die, we die to the Lord. If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s. (Romans 14:8)

This week, please do the thing most people keep putting off: have one “if the day comes” conversation with your family. What medical care do you want, who decides for you, which hymn would you like at the farewell service? And those words “thank you” and “I’m sorry,” do not save them for the funeral hall. Relationships matter more than things; no one on his deathbed wants one more look at his bank book.

Lord Jesus, who died and rose again, we admit that we are afraid, and that there are people we miss so much we cannot speak. Thank You for walking through death Yourself and coming back with the victory. Comfort those who are weeping, let us grieve without despair, and teach us to number our days and live today well. If someone tonight does not want to go on living, hold on to him, send someone to be with him, and give him the courage to speak up today. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
