2. Does the “two rooms” illustration help you, or a bereaved person you have accompanied? Have you ever heard a word of comfort that actually hurt?
3. If you had only one year left, what would you stop and what would you start? Which one can you start on this week?
Yahweh God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.” (Genesis 2:18)
Brothers and sisters, friends, peace! Let me ask you: where was the loneliest you have ever been in your life?

I would guess that for many the answer is not the middle of nowhere. It may be the Lunar New Year, a table full of relatives, you smiling and picking up food, and not one person truly asking how you have been. It may be between husband and wife, two people lying on the same bed, each scrolling their own phone, with a galaxy between them. Or it may, I am sorry to say, be in the church. Everyone is singing “We are one family,” and after the service you walk alone to your scooter.

Today we walk into the fifth gallery of the Life’s Questions Hall, and the topic is “Loneliness.” Let me first say the thing I most want to say: if you are lonely, this is not your sin, and it does not mean something is wrong with your spiritual life. I am not here today to scold you. Let us look together at what this pain is really saying.
1. Loneliness is a kind of thirst

In 2025 a commission of the World Health Organization published a report estimating that around the world one in six people is affected by loneliness, and that deaths associated with loneliness number more than 871,000 a year, which works out to about a hundred every hour. These are extrapolated figures, not counted by name, but they are enough to make us go quiet.

The report also made a very important distinction. Social isolation is objective: you really have few people in your life. Loneliness is subjective: it is the pain from the gap between the relationships you want and the relationships you actually have.

So an elderly grandma who lives alone, who makes the rounds of the market every day and gets a ride to church on Sunday, may not be lonely at all. A company executive with three thousand contacts on his phone, who at two in the morning wants someone to talk to and cannot find a single one, may be terribly lonely.

I like to use an illustration: loneliness is like thirst. A thirsty person has nothing to be ashamed of; it is the body reminding you that it is time to drink. Loneliness is also a signal, reminding you: you are a person who needs relationships.
The body is keeping count too

This signal should not be taken lightly. A 2015 meta-analysis found that loneliness, social isolation and living alone were associated with about twenty-six, twenty-nine and thirty-two percent higher likelihood of death respectively. Another analysis in 2023 pooled 90 cohort studies with about 2.2 million people, and estimated about thirty-two percent for social isolation and about fourteen percent for loneliness.
In 2023 the US Surgeon General also made a comparison that spread widely: the effect of lacking social connection on the risk of early death can be as great as smoking fifteen cigarettes a day.

At this point we have to be honest. These studies are mostly observational, and people cannot be randomly assigned to isolation. Does loneliness make the body worse, or does a worse body make people lonelier? Most likely both, and scientists are still sorting it out. So, everyone, please don't go home and tell your family, “The pastor says that if you don't keep me company, it's like making me smoke fifteen cigarettes.” That would only make you lonelier.
The spiritual meaning: the first “not good”

But the Bible noticed this much earlier than these reports. Open to Genesis 1, everyone. God made the light and saw that it was good; He made the seas, the trees, the birds and the animals, and saw that it was good. Good, good, good, wonderfully good.
By chapter 2, the setting is perfect, sin has not yet entered, and there is no problem between the man and God. Yet God says the first “not good”: it is not good for the man to be alone.

Brothers and sisters, this sentence is very comforting. You need people, not because your spiritual life is not mature enough. Adam needed them before he ever sinned. Needing relationship is the factory setting.
2. He has lived in love from eternity, and He entered the deepest abandonment
God did not make people because He was lonely

Why were people made like this? Here we move from science to faith, and please notice that what follows is theological inference, not an experimental result. To be fair, evolutionary psychology has its explanation too: people need a group to survive, so loneliness, like hunger, urges a person back to the group. This explanation is supported by research and does not need to mention God. Many Christians hold that God can shape human emotions through natural processes. “How it came about” and “what it is for” answer different questions.

The Bible’s answer to “what it is for” is this: if God were alone in eternity, whom would He love? He would have to wait until He had made a world to begin to have an object of love. What the Christian faith says is that the one true God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, has loved one another from eternity. Jesus’ prayer before His arrest reveals this secret.
Father, I desire that they also whom you have given me be with me where I am, that they may see my glory which you have given me, for you loved me before the foundation of the world. (John 17:24)

“You loved me before the foundation of the world.” Everyone, there is a family inside that sentence. God is not a being sitting bored by Himself in the universe who then shaped a few people to keep Him company. His love was so full that it overflowed, so He opened the door and invited us in.

Does this God know what loneliness is? Look at the last day of Jesus’ life. In the Garden of Gethsemane He asked the three closest disciples to stay with Him a while, and they fell asleep. When He was arrested, everyone ran away. At the trial, Peter said he did not know the man. At last on the cross He cried out loudly the words of Psalm 22.
At the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, “Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?” which is, being interpreted, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34)

How deep that cry goes, theologians have been speaking of for two thousand years without finishing. We can only say with reverence: Jesus truly bore our sins and walked into that darkness. The triune God was not thereby divided, but that cry was real.
So, brothers and sisters, when at three in the morning you feel that no one understands, you do not have to explain it to Jesus. He has been to a place deeper than that, and He rose again.
The spiritual meaning: a promise with flesh and blood
Precisely because He walked through abandonment and rose from the dead, Hebrews can say this to us.
For he has said, “I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.” (Hebrews 13:5)

This is not a little card to stick on the refrigerator. It was given in person by the One who has been abandoned. You may not be able to feel Him today, and not feeling Him does not mean He has left. Let us honestly say to Him first, “Lord, I can't feel You right now.” The people in the Psalms often prayed this way, and God did not rebuke them.
3. He places people into a family
Single brothers and sisters are not half persons
Here I want to pause especially. Some people, as soon as they hear “not good to be alone,” start introducing dates to their single friends. Aunties, please put the phone down first.

The immediate context of this verse in Genesis is indeed marriage, but it does not say that single people are incomplete. Our Lord Jesus never married, and the apostle Paul had no spouse during his ministry. Dare you say that they were half persons? And those of you who are married know that marriage does not guarantee you will not be lonely, and your spouse did not marry you to fill every empty place in your heart.
God’s answer is much wider than marriage. Once, when Jesus was told that His mother and brothers were outside looking for Him, He looked at those sitting around Him and said this.
Looking around at those who sat around him, he said, “Behold, my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of God is my brother, my sister, and mother.” (Mark 3:34-35)

The church should be this kind of place: the single, the widowed, the divorced, those who have just arrived from abroad, all have family here. If our small groups only have a seat for couples, that is something we need to repent of, not a problem with them.
Why “get out more” is not quite enough

There is a piece of research that moved me. Lonely people become especially alert to social threat. A coworker does not reply to a message, and he thinks, “He must dislike me.” The small group leader does not greet him, and he thinks, “Sure enough, no one cares about me.” So he steps further back, and it becomes harder for others to reach him. It is a cycle that turns by itself.

A meta-analysis found that the overall effect of ways of reducing loneliness is not large, but methods that address these thoughts work better than simply adding opportunities for social contact. So if you are only dragged along to activities and come home lonelier, you are not strange. Sometimes we need a trustworthy friend, a pastor, or a professional counselor to walk with us and look at those words again. If the low mood has lasted for several weeks, or you already feel you cannot go on, please tell someone today, and also see a doctor or find a counselor. In Taiwan you can call the Peace of Mind Hotline 1925, or Lifeline 1995. Seeking help does not mean your faith is lacking.

In 321 we speak of the 235 relationships: spiritual companions, spiritual parents and children, spiritual comrades. This is not a networking chart; it is what a family ought to look like. Someone walks beside you, someone leads you in front, someone behind needs you, and someone fights the battle with you.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many people have been busy in the church for ten years, with a mountain of ministry, and not a single person knows what is really on their heart. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things.

You do not need all three at once. Today, first pray and ask God to give you one companion. Then be brave and be the one who speaks first. Humility overcomes pride; the four words “I need you” are sometimes harder to say than a whole sermon.

Brothers and sisters, loneliness hurts, and science says this pain should not be taken lightly. The Bible says this pain has an origin: you were made for relationship, and the God who made you Himself walked through abandonment and promises never to leave you.

This week, please do one small thing: invite one person to a meal, or make a twenty-minute phone call, preferably to someone you think may be lonely too: an older person living alone, a single mom or dad, a new friend. No need for big ideas. Just ask, “How have you been lately?” and then listen.
Now please be quiet. Think: at what time of day are you most lonely? Tell Jesus that time.

Let us pray together: Lord Jesus, You were abandoned by everyone, and You understand me. I hand You the loneliness I cannot put into words. Thank You for promising never to leave me. Give me courage to open up to others, and open my eyes to see the people around me who are just as lonely. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
1. Was your loneliest experience when you were alone, or in the middle of a crowd? If you are willing, share the one sentence you most wanted to hear at that time.
2. Of these two lines, “needing relationship is the factory setting” and “I will in no way leave you,” which helps you more in your situation right now? Why?
3. Does our small group or church have places where the single, widowed, divorced or newcomers cannot find a seat? Whom can you reach out to this week?
There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, who don’t walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit. (Romans 8:1)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace! Let me ask: do you remember the most embarrassing moment of your life? No need to raise your hand, and I will not ask you to come up and share. But I guess that the moment I ask, a picture pops into your mind, in very good resolution, and it may be from more than ten years ago. In junior high, the teacher reading your test paper out in front of the whole class. At a wedding banquet, a relative asking, “Why aren’t you married yet?” At the company, the boss calling out your name in public. Or when something happened to your child and you saw a neighbor at the market and took a detour.

Strange, isn’t it? You may have forgotten what you had for lunch yesterday, but that scene you remember perfectly. Today in the sixth gallery of the Life’s Questions Hall, the topic is “Shame and Sin.” We will ask three things: what exactly is shame? How is it related to sin? And what did Jesus do about these two things?
I did something wrong, and I am wrong

Psychologists have done a great deal of research, and there is a distinction that is very useful. A child is caught cheating on an exam. If he says in his heart, “I did something wrong,” that is called guilt. If he says in his heart, “I am just a loser,” that is called shame. The difference is only a few words, but the road that comes out is different. Overall, research finds that guilt is more likely to lead a person to apologize and make amends, while shame is more likely to make a person hide, deny, or even turn on you in anger. Have you met this kind of person, who explodes when you give him a single reminder? Often that is not a bad temper. You have touched the shame inside him.

Let me give you a picture. Guilt is like the warning light on the dashboard: it comes on, and you take the car to be fixed. Shame is someone walking up and patting your car and saying, “This one was always scrap metal.” You will not go to the repair shop. You will hide the car in the garage and never drive it out again.

There is a social work scholar who has studied shame for many years, Brené Brown. She does not start from faith, but she has an observation that the church should hear: shame grows fastest in secrecy. If a person can find a safe person, tell the story, and receive empathy, the power of shame begins to loosen. Isn’t that an interesting echo of what the Bible calls coming to the light? Of course, a psychological observation cannot be used to prove faith. We are only seeing that both sides have noticed the same wound.
Do the Chinese have only face?

You may have heard the saying that the East is a shame culture and the West a guilt culture. It comes from The Chrysanthemum and the Sword, written by Ruth Benedict in 1946. She was doing analysis for the US government in wartime, could not go to Japan at the time, and the book has since been criticized by quite a few scholars. We should not be quick to stick on that label. A scholar who did research in Taiwan, Bedford, interviewed Taiwanese people and, for shame alone, analyzed the words diulian, cankui, xiukui and xiuchi, and for guilt the words neijiu, zui’e gan and fanzui gan. The Chinese conscience is not dull at all; it is just that we do care a lot about other people’s eyes.

There is another problem we often meet in sharing the gospel. You tell a friend, “You are a sinner,” and he answers right back, “But I haven’t broken the law!” Yes, he is right, because the Chinese word for sin sounds like going to court. We have to explain patiently that what the Bible calls sin is more like a broken relationship: the Master of this world is right before our eyes, and I live as though He did not exist, putting myself in the center.
The spiritual meaning: shame is a signal, not a verdict

Shame is not entirely bad in itself. The prophet Jeremiah rebuked the people of his day because they “were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush.” For a person to do something that hurts others and feel nothing at all, that is what is frightening. So shame is sometimes like the sense of pain, reminding us that something has gone wrong. But pain is there to remind you to see a doctor, not to pronounce a death sentence on you. Today many people take the signal for a verdict and live inside it all their lives.

Let us turn to Genesis. The last sentence of chapter 2 is very beautiful: “The man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.” Fully seen, and completely unafraid. This is how human beings were originally set up. Then in chapter 3, the serpent says one thing: “you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” Did you hear it? The root of the problem is here. People did not want to be people; they wanted to be God. This is what we often call being self-centered: leaving one’s place and grasping a position that does not belong to us.
Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves. (Genesis 3:7)

Their eyes were opened, and what they saw was that they had no clothes on. Everyone, our leaves today are a lot more upscale. Degrees are leaves, fancy cars are leaves, children’s grades are leaves, and photos in the friends’ feed are leaves. In church, “I’m fine, thank the Lord” is sometimes a leaf too. Leaves have a problem: they dry out. So you have to keep sewing, until you are exhausted.
The next passage is one of the gentlest in the whole Bible. The man hid behind the trees. What did God do? He did not send down a thunderbolt. He walked into the garden and asked:
Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9)

Does God need to locate them? No. This line is like a father who knows perfectly well that his child is hiding behind the curtain, with his feet sticking out, and still asks gently, “Sweetheart, where are you?” He wants you to come out by yourself. Afterward God of course spoke of the consequences; the consequences of sin are real, and He did not pretend that nothing had happened. But the story ends with this line: Yahweh God made garments of animal skins and clothed them. The leaves they sewed themselves were replaced with clothes God made with His own hands.
The spiritual meaning: pride and shame are the same coin

Brothers and sisters, a proud person feels better than others, and a person in shame feels worse than others. They look opposite, but both are keeping their eyes fixed on themselves. So the way to deal with shame is not to pump in more self-confidence. The way is to give the place back to God: letting God be God and people be people. When you no longer need to be God, you no longer need to be a perfect person either.
He walked toward the most shameful place

Today when we look at the cross, it is a necklace, a mark on a church roof, and already quite respectable. But in the Roman world of the first century, the cross was the least respectable word there was. The scholar Martin Hengel wrote a book devoted to the history of this, and he points out that crucifixion was, besides being cruel, bound up with extreme disgrace. And the Bible says it just so: those passing by reviled Him and wagged their heads, telling Him to come down. Everyone, that was the most public disgrace in the whole city.

looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God. (Hebrews 12:2)

“Despising its shame.” These words deserve a longer look. It is not that He could not feel it. He made the shame small, because there was a greater joy before Him. What was that joy? It is you. It is bringing you and me home. Hebrews also says that He is not ashamed to call us brothers. Think about it: the you that you most fear people will find out, Jesus knows, and He is still not ashamed of you.

In Luke 15 the prodigal son came home with a confession speech prepared. What did the father do before he had finished listening? The text says that while he was still far off, his father saw him, and ran, and fell on his neck. Kenneth Bailey, who studied Middle Eastern culture, points out that in that society an elder of standing would not run in the street; to run he would have to hitch up his robe, which was very undignified. This is an interpretation, not something the text says outright, but I love the picture: the father rushed out ahead of the whole village’s shaming of his son, and lost face himself first. Then he told them to bring the best robe, a ring and sandals. That was the restoration of identity, with all the leaves replaced.
The spiritual meaning: forgiving sin, and removing shame

So we need to be clear. If I did something wrong, the gospel’s road is confession. First John says, “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins.” Please notice that His forgiveness is righteous, because Christ has paid the price. But after confessing, many people still cannot get out of shame, and for that we must hear Romans 8:1: “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus.” The judge’s verdict has been announced, and you do not need to hold court on yourself every day.

David also walked this road. In Psalm 32 he said, “When I kept silence, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long.” That is a vivid picture: holding your mouth shut and holding on until your bones dry up. Later he said, “I acknowledged my sin to you. I didn’t hide my iniquity.” And you forgave. Everyone, confession is not shaming yourself one more time, and it does not require standing on a platform for public execution. Confession is opening the door and letting the doctor in.

I also want to say a few words especially to some of you, so please listen carefully. For some people, shame did not come from doing something wrong; it came from being assaulted, abused at home, bullied, or scolded from childhood. The Bible records that after David’s daughter Tamar was raped by her brother, she put ashes on her head and wept aloud, while her family told her to hold her peace. That is a tragedy, not an example. Please hear this clearly: it is not your fault. Being a victim is not a sin, and you do not need to repent of it. If you are still in danger, seek safety first, find someone you trust, and find professional help; in Taiwan you can call 113. Doing this is not a lack of faith. And the church, please remember, must never tell the wounded to be quiet.

Brothers and sisters, the first of the three foundations: Jesus is my example. How did He treat shame? To the Samaritan woman He pointed out her past line by line, yet He did not shame her, and the woman ran back to the city and said to everyone, “Come, see.” The thing she feared most that people would know became her testimony. This is the road from self-centered to selfless: no longer managing an “I,” because “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”

This week, please do one thing: think of one thing that is hard for you, and ask yourself, is it “I did something wrong,” or “someone hurt me”? If I did something wrong, go and confess, apologize, make amends. If someone hurt me, go and tell a trusted person or a professional counselor. What shame fears most is the light, and as soon as you say even a small part, it has already begun to shrink.
Now please be quiet. Bring that scene before God. Hear Him asking: “Where are you?”

Let us pray together: Heavenly Father, I often hide. I cover myself with many leaves, and I am truly tired. For the things I have done wrong I confess to You today and ask You to forgive, and give me courage to make amends. As for the hurt and disgrace that others laid on me, I will not carry it for them any more; please heal me Yourself. Thank You, Lord Jesus, that You despised the shame and went to the cross and are not ashamed of me. Today I am willing to come out. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
1. In your culture or family, what is the sentence you hear most often that makes people ashamed? How has it affected you?
2. What is your “fig leaf” today? Achievements, image, busyness, or “I’m fine”?
3. How can our small group become a place where people dare to tell the truth? What words or practices make wounded people even less willing to speak?
Are Money and Success Enough? The Navigation That Keeps Jumping to the Next Stop
He said to them, “Beware! Keep yourselves from covetousness, for a man’s life doesn’t consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses.” (Luke 12:15)
Brothers and sisters, peace to you! Today I want to say something that a lot of pastors are afraid to say outright: money really does help.

I know, you may have assumed that I would open the Bible today and tell you that money is the root of all evil, that rich people are all empty inside, and that being a little poor is more spiritual. Friends, if your child has a high fever and you have only a hundred NT dollars left in your pocket, you will not feel that poverty is very spiritual. You will only want to run to the ATM, and then find that there is nothing in there either. So this message has to begin by removing an illusion. We are not going to preach the kind of sermon in which someone in designer leather shoes tells everyone else to look down on money.

But I am not going to tell you either that if you give enough offerings, God will let you drive a Mercedes. That teaching is even worse than the first. Today we will walk the narrower road in the middle. We will see what the research says and what the Bible says, and then ask a very practical question: how much is actually enough?
1. First, an honest word: money really does help
The logic of the phone battery

In 2010 two Nobel laureates, Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton, analyzed more than 450,000 survey responses in the United States. They found that people’s evaluation of their own lives kept climbing with income, but their everyday mood stopped improving once income reached about 75,000 US dollars a year. That number became famous around the world, and many people used it to say: see, once you earn up to a certain point, it is enough.

The story is not over. In 2021 a younger scholar, Matthew Killingsworth, used a phone app to ask people at random moments how they felt right then. He collected more than a million responses, and the result was that mood kept rising with income, with no 75,000 ceiling at all. By the usual script in academia, what should come next is that both sides write articles and open fire. Instead Kahneman did something very admirable. He sat down with the other side, brought in a third party as a go-between, and they recalculated together. In 2023 they published jointly and said that the least happy group of people did level off after a certain income, but that most other people’s happiness kept increasing with the logarithm of their income.

What is a logarithm? Think of your phone battery. Charge it from one percent to twenty percent and you come back to life: the call goes through and the map works. Charge it from eighty to one hundred and it is nice, you just feel a little more secure. To feel one more notch of the same happiness, your income has to double again. So for a person who is still at one percent, money is a lifeline. We must never say to that person, “Brother, money can’t buy happiness.” That sentence is usually spoken by people who are above eighty percent.
What happened to the lottery winners

Even more interesting is the Swedish study. They surveyed big-prize lottery winners, asked them again anywhere from five to twenty-two years after the win, and compared them with people in similar circumstances. Guess what? The story we preachers would love to hear is that the winners all went bankrupt, got divorced and had regrets. The research tells us it did not go that way. Their satisfaction with life as a whole stayed higher, and even after more than ten years there was no clear fading.

But the gap in the happiness and mental health of that same group was much smaller. The researchers think that a large part of the extra satisfaction was satisfaction with their financial situation. In plain language: he no longer has to worry about the bills, and that is a really good thing, thank the Lord. It is just that the thing that sits in your chest when you wake up in the middle of the night may not be the bills.
He who loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver, nor he who loves abundance, with increase. This also is vanity. (Ecclesiastes 5:10)
The spiritual meaning: poverty is not a virtue, and wealth is not a sign

The Lausanne Movement’s Theology Working Group met in Akropong, Ghana, in Africa and issued a statement on prosperity teaching. Our brothers and sisters in Africa know better than anyone how deeply this teaching has hurt people. On the one hand they affirm that the Bible places material well-being within God’s blessing, and that God takes no pleasure in people living in poverty. On the other hand they clearly reject the idea that wealth must mean God is pleased with you, and that poverty, illness and early death must mean a curse or too little faith.
So, brothers and sisters, if someone has ever told you, “You got sick because you didn’t give enough,” let me apologize to you on behalf of that sentence. That is not the gospel.
2. The navigation that jumps to the next stop by itself

There is one good thing about phone navigation. When you reach the destination it says, “You have arrived,” and then goes quiet. The navigation of life is not like that. The moment you arrive, it jumps to the next stop by itself.

You get into a good school: you have arrived, next stop, a good major. You join a good company: next stop, manager. You become a manager: next stop, director. You buy a house: next stop, a bigger one. Your child is born: next stop, your child’s good school. You see, we go around the circle and come back to the first stop, except that this time the one sitting in the driver’s seat is your child.
The author of Ecclesiastes ran this whole road long ago. He built houses, planted vineyards and piled up silver and gold, and when he had finished, he wrote down this report.

Then I looked at all the works that my hands had worked, and at the labor that I had labored to do; and behold, all was vanity and a chasing after wind, and there was no profit under the sun. (Ecclesiastes 2:11)

Psychology calls this adaptation. People gradually get used to what they already have. The smell of a new car fades before long, and you no longer feel grateful every time you get in. To be fair, adaptation is not one hundred percent; the Swedish study corrected the overly dramatic claims of the early research. But that navigation that keeps jumping to the next stop by itself should be familiar to all of us.
The account of bringing glory to the ancestors

We Chinese have one more layer. The Classic of Filial Piety says: “To establish oneself and walk in the Way, to make one’s name known to later generations and so bring honor to one’s parents: this is the final stage of filial piety.” Let me say first that being grateful to our parents is a beautiful thing, and the Bible tells us to honor our father and mother. Many parents scrimp and save, do not allow themselves to buy a single piece of clothing, and pay for their children’s schooling. We want to make their faces shine, and that is love.

But sometimes this love turns into a debt that can never be paid off. The Taiwanese psychologist Kuang-Hui Yeh and his colleague Olwen Bedford distinguished two kinds of filial piety: one that comes out of affection and repays love, and one that comes out of role and authority and demands obedience. There are people in their forties, successful in their careers, who still go to class reunions and calculate whether they measure up. There are people who are really good at painting but have worked in a bank for twenty years, because back then their father said, “Can you eat painting?” You may have also seen this scene: a child comes home with a doctorate, and the first thing the elder asks is, “Isn’t so-and-so’s child already a professor?” Elders like that mostly do love their children; they grew up that way themselves. Friends, this navigation is handed down from one generation to the next.
The spiritual meaning: who set my price?

From here we can see the heart of the problem. Achievement itself is good, and diligence is a virtue too. God gave you talents precisely so that you would use them well. The trouble is that we often use achievement to answer a question it cannot answer: am I worth being loved? Once you hand that question to achievement, you can never clock out.
3. Where was the man a fool?
A few short sentences, five times “I”

Jesus told the story of a rich man. Notice that this man did not steal and did not rob; his harvest grew out of his own fields. He was not lazy either. He even made a plan to expand, and today he could be on the cover of a business magazine.

But listen closely to what he says to himself. “What will I do, because I don’t have room to store my crops?” “This is what I will do. I will pull down my barns, build bigger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. I will tell my soul…” I have counted: in just a few lines of the Chinese Union Version, the word “I” appears five times. No God, no poor people, no coworkers, not even family. He is holding a board meeting at which he is the only one present.

“But God said to him, ‘You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you. The things which you have prepared—whose will they be?’ So is he who lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.” (Luke 12:20-21)

Notice that Jesus does not scold him for being rich. Jesus says he is a fool. Where is the foolishness? He stored the hope of a man who will die in a warehouse he cannot take with him. This is a sum worked out wrongly. No wonder Jesus also asked another question: “For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his life?”
God richly provides us with everything

So may a Christian not earn money? Paul’s word to Timothy is very balanced. He says, “For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.” Many people memorize it as “money is the root of all evil,” and dropping those words changes a great deal. He also said the following, which I love.

Charge those who are rich in this present age that they not be arrogant, nor have their hope set on the uncertainty of riches, but on the living God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy; (1 Timothy 6:17)

“Everything to enjoy,” the Bible says! So when you eat a good meal or take your family on a trip, you may give thanks to God with a clear conscience. As for giving, the Old Testament teaches the tithe, and Malachi has his words about the windows of heaven opening. Those words were addressed to the Israel of that day and to their temple. Jesus also reminded the Pharisees that the tithe should not be left undone, but that the weightier matters are justice, mercy and faith. Giving is gratitude and not an investment; you cannot treat God as a fund with guaranteed returns. The Lausanne statement specifically points out the harm done when “sowing seed” language goes bad. Willing giving is practice in opening the hand, and it is also telling our own heart: my Lord is not Mammon.
The spiritual meaning: He became poor for you

So who will answer that question? Am I worth being loved? The gospel’s answer is this. Peter says you were redeemed “not with corruptible things like silver or gold,” but “with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish or spot, the blood of Christ.” Friends, what a thing is worth depends on what someone is willing to pay for it. What God paid for you was His Son.
For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich. (2 Corinthians 8:9)

This price was set before you passed the exam, and it will not drop after you lose your job. A person who knows their worth is already settled can work very hard and can also stop; can earn a lot and can also give a lot. Zacchaeus was like that. When Jesus came to his house as a guest, he was not asked to, and he stood up on his own and said he would give half of his goods to the poor. The money had not changed. The hand that was gripping it had relaxed.

We often talk about the self-centered life and the selfless life. In a self-centered life, even giving is to get one’s money back, even filial piety is for face, and even serving is for results. Selflessness does not mean putting your career away, and it does not mean deliberately living a hard life. It means vacating the throne so that Jesus reigns and money goes back to being the servant. We move from the human, temporary measuring stick to God’s eternal one.

This week, please do one small thing. Find a person or a need and quietly give an amount of money or time that you can slightly feel, anonymously and without posting about it. Then write down what came up in your heart as you let go. If what comes up is reluctance, congratulations, you have found your barn, and the Lord is ready to help you right there. If you are short of money right now, please do not feel pressure. The most spiritual thing today may be to open your mouth and let your brothers and sisters help you, because that is exactly how the church is meant to care for one another.

Let us pray together. Heavenly Father, You richly provide us with everything to enjoy, and I thank You for all You have given me. Forgive me for staking my worth on numbers and titles, and for using achievement to settle my account with my parents and with myself. Lord Jesus, You became poor for me. Be my true wealth, so that my hands can grasp and also let go. For those who are worried about their bills right now, please provide for them Yourself, and send us to be Your hands. In Jesus’ name, amen.
1. Which stop has the navigation of your life jumped to now? After you arrive, where do you expect it to jump next?
2. How does your family define “success”? What blessing has that definition brought you, and what burden?

3. The Lausanne statement rejects both “wealth is a sign of blessing” and “poverty is a lack of faith.” Which of these two ideas has influenced you more? How would you like to practice letting go this week?
Forgiveness: Write Off the Bad Debt, Don’t Move Back Into the Unsafe Building
And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you. (Ephesians 4:32)
Brothers and sisters, there is a sentence that has harmed a lot of people: “You’re a Christian. You have to forgive him and go back.”

The people who say this are often well-meaning elders, Bible in hand, with a gentle tone. The person who hears it may still have bruises on her arm. So this message on forgiveness begins in the place least like a sermon.

If today you are being beaten, threatened or controlled, or if your child is being hurt, the first half of this message was prepared for you, and it has only one sentence: please go to a safe place first. You do not have to forgive first, and you do not have to check first whether you are spiritual enough. In Taiwan you can call 113, and someone answers twenty-four hours a day. In Singapore it is 1800-777-0000. In Malaysia it is 15999. In New Zealand you can call 0800 733 843 or 0800 456 450. If there is immediate danger, call the police. The World Health Organization estimated in 2025 that nearly one in three women worldwide experiences partner violence or sexual violence in her lifetime. You are not alone, and it is not your fault.
If anyone in the church has ever urged you to endure, or to stay for the sake of the children or for the sake of your witness, I want to say to you here: I am sorry. That is not what Jesus meant.
The parable of the bad debt

All right, now let us talk about forgiveness. I will start with an accounting term: writing off a bad debt. Those of you in business will understand. A sum of money has been defaulted on. The other person really does owe you, and the books record it clearly; you are not unaware of it. But one day you decide that you will no longer phone every day to collect, and no longer let this account take over the time when you eat, sleep and drive. So you write it off the books.

Notice three things. First, writing off a bad debt does not mean the other person does not owe you. Second, writing off a bad debt does not mean you will lend him another million. Third, if his conduct breaks the law, the prosecutor can still bring charges. Forgiveness is the same. You forgive precisely because the thing was wrong; if it were not wrong, there would be nothing to forgive.

The psychologist Everett Worthington, who has studied forgiveness for decades, has a vivid way of putting it. He says forgiveness is something that happens inside your own skin. Whether justice is done is a separate matter. A person can forgive an abuser and at the same time refuse to reconcile with someone who is still dangerous. He has the right to say this. His own mother was killed in a home invasion, and the killer was never prosecuted.
The parable of the unsafe building

Let me give you a second picture. An earthquake has damaged a building, and the walls are cracked. One day you can stop splashing paint at the developer’s door, and that is your own business; your heart can be set free first. But whether to move back in is not decided by feeling. A structural engineer has to inspect it. If the engineer has not signed off, anyone who urges you to move back is harming you.

Forgiveness is no longer splashing paint, and reconciliation is moving back in. The first one a person can do alone. The second takes two people, and the other person must truly change. A “sorry” is not the engineer’s signature, and a few flowers are not the engineer’s signature. Even tearful weeping does not count. What we look for is change over a long time, with someone watching.

I am not saying this too harshly. A 2011 study followed newlywed couples and found that when one spouse was more inclined to forgive, the partner’s aggression was more likely to continue. Robert Enright, a pioneer of forgiveness research, criticized that study as too thin, because “forgiveness” was never defined on the questionnaire, and the respondents may well have been condoning. Friends, however much the two sides argue, they point to the same thing: when forgiveness is treated as condoning, people keep getting hurt.
The spiritual meaning: running away is in the Bible too
Saul sought to pin David to the wall with the spear, but he slipped away out of Saul’s presence; and he stuck the spear into the wall. David fled and escaped that night. (1 Samuel 19:10)

David did not stay there for the sake of his witness. When Paul was being hunted, the disciples let him down over the city wall in a basket. In Nazareth, when people wanted to throw Jesus off a cliff, He passed through the midst of them. Jesus’ cross is a road He willingly walked for us, and it is completely different from being beaten by one’s family. Please do not let anyone confuse the two.

Jesus also taught that when a brother sins against you, you should “show him his fault”; if he does not listen, take others along; if he still does not listen, tell the church. So forgiveness in the Bible has never included covering things up. If someone in the church has been harmed, especially a child, the first move of a small group leader or pastor is to protect, and to report as the law requires.
The debt that was 600,000 times larger

So why does the Bible still tell us to forgive? Peter asked Jesus, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?” He probably thought he was being very generous. Jesus answered, seventy times seven, and then told a story.

The Chinese Union Version translates “ten million taels of silver”; the original is ten thousand talents, and the fellow servant’s “ten taels of silver” is a hundred denarii. By the usual conversion one talent equals six thousand denarii, so the two debts differ by about 600,000 times. A man owed so much that selling his whole family could not repay it, and his master wiped it out with a word. As soon as he went out, he met a fellow servant, grabbed him by the throat, and demanded that little sum.

Then his lord called him in and said to him, ‘You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt because you begged me. Shouldn’t you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?’ (Matthew 18:32-33)

This parable is heavy, and I do not want to make it light. But notice that it was told to Peter, to a man who was getting ready to count the number of times. It was never a stick for driving a scarred person back home. God’s grace, once it has come to us, must flow outward. When and how we walk this road should be entrusted to the Holy Spirit, and there should be someone walking with us.
The cold hand, and the tears still flowing

Corrie ten Boom’s sister died in the Ravensbrück concentration camp. In 1947, after she had spoken about forgiveness in Munich, a man who had been a guard at the camp came up to her, said that he had become a believer, and held out his hand, asking her to forgive him. She wrote that her heart was cold at that moment, and she could only pray that the Lord would help her lift her hand. After her hand was lifted, she felt a warmth flood in.

Many people love the ending of this story. I would like you to notice its beginning: her heart was ice. Feelings often come more slowly than decisions. As for the warm flood, please do not take it as a standard either. You may lift your hand and still be cold, and that does not mean you have failed.

Now think of the Amish. In 2006, in the Pennsylvania school shooting, five girls were killed and five seriously wounded. They quickly extended forgiveness to the killer’s widow and family, and the world was stunned. But ten years later, when reporters returned, the grief was still there, and a child was still in a wheelchair. One father said he had been freed from anger and bitterness but not freed from the pain. Their community also said that forgiveness is a journey, and that they need to help one another hold on to the decision.

So if you forgive today and tomorrow morning you remember and hate again, that does not mean yesterday was fake. The last of Worthington’s five REACH steps is called Hold on. There was a 2024 randomized trial in Hong Kong, Indonesia, Colombia, South Africa and Ukraine, in which more than four thousand five hundred people used a self-guided workbook. After two weeks their feelings of unforgiveness went down, with a much smaller help for depression and anxiety, and they were followed for only two weeks. A very honest result: forgiveness helps, and it is not a cure-all.

South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission is an example many people love to cite, with Archbishop Tutu as chair. Of more than seven thousand one hundred amnesty applications, eight hundred and forty-nine were granted, on the condition that they fully tell what they had done. For many victims it was the first time they could speak publicly. But the family of Steve Biko also took the case to the highest court, saying they had been robbed of the right to seek justice. I do not intend to rule on that for them. Friends, one nation’s reconciliation cannot be used to make demands on the heart of any single victim.
The spiritual meaning: vengeance belongs to God
Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.” (Romans 12:19)

You can lay down the gavel because the court is still in session, and there is a Judge who will judge. If there were no final judgment, telling a victim to let go would be too cruel. The Bible also says that the authority is a servant of God, “an avenger for wrath to him who does evil.” So handing the case to God and handing it to the court do not conflict.
3. The cross, and letting yourself go
He was wounded to the very end

When Jesus was crucified, He said, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” We often remember only how loving He was and forget the situation in which He said it. The nails were real, the shame was real, and His friends had run away. So when you come before Him with your wounds, you will not hear “it’s nothing.” He knows.
On the cross sin was not lightly passed over. God’s justice and love meet here. That deepest wound, He carried Himself, and He also passed judgment on it.
The spiritual meaning: no longer acting as your own prosecutor

For some people the name they most cannot let go of is their own. That phone call you did not answer, that thing you said to your child, that relationship that should never have begun. In the deep of the night the prosecutor is in session again, and knows the whole case by heart.

Here we have to separate two kinds of people. If you have truly hurt someone, please confess, take responsibility and make amends as best you can, and do not press the other person to forgive you quickly. That is a second injury. Then return the authority to condemn to God.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. (1 John 1:9)

And there is another kind of person, who after being harmed keeps blaming herself: was it what I wore, was I not good enough, was it my fault that my child saw. Friends, that is not your sin. You do not need to be forgiven; you need to be comforted, and you need professional help. “Yahweh is near to those who have a broken heart.”

We often speak of selflessness. I want to be especially clear that selflessness is never allowing yourself to be trampled on. It means no longer making yourself the center, and it does not cancel your dignity. Letting God be God means returning the judge’s seat to Him, and it also means not treating anyone who strikes you as God.

This week, please take just one small step: tell a trustworthy, mature Christian or a counseling professional that there is an account in your heart you cannot let go of. You are not asked to let go today. If you are in danger right now, your first step is that phone call.

Let us pray together. Lord Jesus, You know what wounds I have borne, and You were wounded to the very end. I bring this account to You. I may not be able to let go yet, so please help me. Protect those who are in danger now, give them courage to ask for help, and make our church a safe place for them. Forgive me for the ways I have hurt others, so that I no longer act as my own prosecutor. In Jesus’ name, amen.

Love and Family: The Warmest Place, the Most Painful Place
We love him, because he first loved us. (1 John 4:19)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! Let me start with a question: where does the person in the whole world who most easily makes you angry live? That’s right, usually in your own house. At the office you can smile through three meetings in a row, and then you get home, and one sentence, “Why didn’t you put your socks away again?”, can be heard by the whole building.

People outside see us dressed and put together. Our family sees the no-makeup version. That is why home is so strange: it is the place where we are loved most deeply, and so often the place where we hurt others and are hurt the most.

Among the friends sitting here today, some smile when they think of home. Some feel their stomach tighten. And some are going home right now to just one lamp and a refrigerator. Whichever of these you are, this message was prepared for you.
Today we will look through research, look through the Bible, and finally see a Father.
1. The power of family is greater than we think
More than eighty years of following people

Harvard has a famous study of adult development that began in 1938 and followed 724 people: one group of Harvard students and one group of young men from Boston. The researchers followed them into old age, and now they are even following their descendants.

The current director, Robert Waldinger, tells us something. They looked back at all the data and asked: which measurement at age fifty best shows who will be healthy and happy at eighty? Everyone assumed it would be cholesterol, or blood pressure. In fact the best predictor was how satisfied they were with their relationships, especially marriage.

Friends, we still have to look after our cholesterol, and see the doctor when we should. This is observational research, and we cannot say that good relationships guarantee a long life. But it reminds us of one thing: you may think you are working overtime for this family, and sometimes all this family wants is for you to sit down and have a proper meal.
Old braising sauce and dish soap

Let us look at another study. In 1992 the psychologists Gottman and Levenson had couples sit down and talk about their conflicts, recorded every interaction, and followed up four years later. Among 73 couples, those whose interactions were more stable had a ratio of positive to negative behavior close to five to one; those heading toward instability had only about one to one.

I have to be honest: this study had few couples, and they were all American, so five to one is no marriage formula. Please do not go home with a scoreboard. The claim going around that “an expert can tell in a few minutes who will divorce” has been clarified even by the Gottman Institute itself. But there is a direction worth listening to: a good relationship is nourished by a great many everyday kindnesses.

It is very much like a pot of old braising sauce. A good sauce is not made in a day; you add a little each day and the flavor slowly deepens. A “thank you,” a cup of warm water, a “you’ve worked hard today”: these are all ingredients.

What did they find hurts the most? Contempt. The eye-roll, the smirk, the line “that’s all you are.” Contempt is like a spoonful of dish soap: pour it in, and no amount of ingredients can cover the taste. Criticism says, “You did this thing wrong.” Contempt says, “You are not worth anything.”
A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. (Proverbs 15:1)
The spiritual meaning: love is not a savings account of feelings, it is a daily choice

The Bible spoke of this long ago. First Corinthians 13 is a chapter many people have only heard at weddings, but those words were not written for people in wedding clothes. They were written for a church in an uproar. “Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud.” Look closely and you will see that it is almost all verbs, things you can do when you walk through the door tonight.
2. God sees the wounds of the family

But for some people, home is more than a matter of quarrels. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention compiled surveys from 2011 to 2020: about sixty-four percent of adults had at least one adverse experience in childhood, such as abuse, witnessing domestic violence, or parental conflict, and seventeen percent had four or more. These are American numbers, and I will not force them onto Chinese people. But the pastoral field tells us that Chinese families have the same wounds, only that we speak of them even less.

Our culture is very good at saying that family shame must not be made public. And the result? The wounds are like the old pipes in an old house: you cannot see them usually, but when the water pressure rises, they leak. Have you found yourself shouting at your child a sentence exactly like the one your father shouted at you? That is the pipe leaking.

If you pretend nothing is leaking, the ceiling will come down sooner or later. But there is no need to tear down the whole house either, saying “this is just how I am, my parents did this to me.” Find someone who knows the work and repair it one section at a time: a mature spiritual elder, a professional counselor, and confession before God one thing at a time. Research speaks of risk, not destiny. Someone who was hurt is not therefore destined to hurt others.
If there is violence at home

For this next part I am going to slow down, because someone here may need to hear it. The World Health Organization’s 2025 estimate is that nearly one in three women worldwide experiences partner violence or sexual violence in her lifetime. Men and children can be victims too. It also happens in Christian homes.

If this is your situation, please hear me clearly: it is not your fault. When First Corinthians says love “bears all things,” and the Chinese Union Version says it “endures all things,” it does not tell you to stay under a fist. That passage describes what love looks like, and the one who strikes is the one who is not living out the passage. No one may use the Bible to tell you to keep being beaten for the sake of your witness.
Yahweh examines the righteous, but his soul hates the wicked and him who loves violence. (Psalm 11:5)

Your safety comes first, and your children’s safety comes first. In Taiwan please call the 113 Protection Hotline; someone answers twenty-four hours a day. If life is in immediate danger, call 110. Elsewhere, please call the local emergency number. Brothers and sisters in the church, if someone opens up to you, please believe them first and go with them to find professional help. Do not simply tell them to go back and pray harder.
The spiritual meaning: He will not break a bruised reed

Isaiah speaks of the Lord’s servant: “He won’t break a bruised reed. He won’t quench a dimly burning wick.” Brothers and sisters, you may feel that you are that reed, that nearly burned-out lamp. Our Lord is extremely gentle with people like this. He is in no hurry to lecture you. He shields you first.
Filial piety needs an order too

When we talk about family, Chinese people have to talk about filial piety. Many friends worry: does believing in Jesus make us unfilial? Let me tell you, Jesus was very strict about filial piety. In his day some religious people told their parents: this money I have already given to God, so I cannot support you. Jesus rebuked them to their faces and said they were making void the word of God.

Now look at the cross. Hanging there, with His whole weight on the nails, He said to His mother, “Woman, behold, your son!” And to His disciple, “Behold, your mother!” Where in the world is there a son like that?

But He also said that we must not love our parents more than Him. How do we understand that? The Taiwanese scholar Kuang-Hui Yeh, who studies filial piety, separates two kinds: one out of affection, and one out of the demands of role and authority. Both are called filial piety, but one says “I love you” and the other says “I fear you.” When God sits back in God’s place, parents no longer have to be obeyed as gods, and we can love them truly with a freer heart.
No one is a second-class member of the family

And there are friends who, every time the church talks about family, want to hide in the restroom. You are single, you are divorced, you have lost your spouse, you wanted children and do not have any. Let me say this plainly: in God’s family you are not missing a piece. Our Lord Jesus Himself never married, and when Paul wrote 1 Corinthians 7 he had no spouse either (7:7-8; whether he had ever been married is debated among scholars). Jesus once stretched out His hand toward His disciples and said, “Behold, my mother and my brothers!” Beyond blood, there is a larger family. If the church only knows how to ask you, “Why aren’t you married yet?”, that is something we owe you an apology for.

But he answered him who spoke to him, “Who is my mother? Who are my brothers?” He stretched out his hand toward his disciples, and said, “Behold, my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother.” (Matthew 12:48-50)
The spiritual meaning: the Father who runs

Finally I want to talk about the word “Father.” I know that some people tense up as soon as they hear it. Your father may have been always away, or never satisfied, or even struck you. How can I ask you to call God “Father”? Brothers and sisters, God does not blame you for your hesitation.

The Bible does not ask you to imagine God after the pattern of your father. The Bible says, “When my father and my mother forsake me, then Yahweh will take me up.” It honestly admits that earthly parents can fail. Then Jesus told a story. The younger son had squandered the property, and came back looking defeated, rehearsing his lines, thinking he would settle for being a hired servant. “But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him.” That father had been watching the road all along.

To bring us home, this Father paid with His only beloved Son. Christ gave Himself on the cross and rose three days later, opening a road for us who left home. So Paul says: “For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption.”

So how do we live when we go home? We often speak of the order of relationships: God first, then myself, then people, and tasks last. Many family problems come from an order that has been scrambled. If I try to get from my spouse a security that only God can give, of course the other person cannot supply it. Let Jesus reign first, be loved enough by God first, and when we get home we will have less need to win.

We also often speak of 920: every relationship is my 2, I lay myself down to become the 0, and I let the Holy Spirit bring forth the 9 fruits. At home this saying is the hardest, and the truest. When a couple quarrels, the self-centered person asks, “Who is right?” and the selfless person asks, “How do we get back to each other?” Selflessness does not mean letting yourself be trampled, and it certainly does not mean that for someone who is being abused. Selflessness means laying down the “I” that must win, and letting Christ live in me.

This week’s action is small: every day, say one specific word of thanks to a family member. Not “you’re great,” but “thank you for waiting up for me last night.” Add a little ingredient each day. If home makes you afraid, please do something else this week: tell a trusted person about your situation, or call a professional helping agency. That is love too, love for yourself and for your children.

Let us be quiet for a moment, and draw a map of your home in your mind. Which room is the warmest? Which door has always been closed? You do not need to tidy it up first; just lay it open before God as it is.

Let us pray together. Heavenly Father, thank You for loving me first. You know how much warmth my home holds, and how much pain. Heal the places I cannot put into words. Give me wisdom to tell what to forgive and what to ask help for, and teach me to love those around me with the self-giving love of Christ. In Jesus’ name, amen.

Are All Religions the Same? A Beggar’s Answer
Jesus said to him, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me. (John 14:6)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! When you go home for the Lunar New Year, if you are the only one in the family who believes in Jesus, you have probably heard this sentence: “All religions are the same. They all teach people to be good. Why make such a big distinction?” The one who says it is usually an elder, a piece of chicken pinched in chopsticks, speaking in a kindly tone. How will you answer?

Some people answer too fast: “No, they’re not the same! Only Jesus is real!” And then the reunion dinner gets harder to swallow. Others smile and say, “Yes, yes, all the same,” and feel a little guilty inside. Today we want to find a third way: to speak honestly, and to speak gently.

Let me first say a fair word. People who say “all religions are the same” mostly do not want to start trouble. They want peace. In our world the neighbor follows the Buddha, the coworker is Muslim, Mom and Dad go to the temple to burn incense and pray, and the child’s classmate believes in nothing at all. According to Pew Research Center, in 2020 Christians were about twenty-nine percent of the world’s people, Muslims about twenty-six percent, and those with no religious affiliation about twenty-four percent. We all have to live on the same planet and want peace, and we should respect that intention.
1. The blind men and the elephant: the story is not finished

The story most often used to illustrate this is the blind men and the elephant. Several blind men touch an elephant. The one who touches the leg says the elephant is like a pillar, the one who touches the ear says it is like a winnowing basket, the one who touches the tail says it is like a broom. So what? Everyone has touched only a part, everyone is right and everyone is incomplete, so stop arguing.

What is interesting is that this story appears very early in the Buddhist scripture called the Udāna. There the setting is this: some ascetics were quarreling fiercely over their views, and the Buddha told his disciples this story. A king had men born blind gathered to touch an elephant. Each said his own thing, and in the end they actually came to blows, while the king watched with great amusement. The Buddha’s conclusion was that these people, seeing only one side, fight one another.

Did you notice, friends? The original story does not say that “everyone is right.” The Buddha was criticizing those who could not see. We should respect the original text, and not speak for the Buddha.
The one who saw the whole elephant

There is one more small detail in this story, and I ask you to think about it. Who knows that those people all touched only a part? Someone has to be standing to the side, eyes bright, seeing the whole elephant, to be able to say it. So when we say, “No one sees the whole picture,” that sentence is already a declaration about the whole picture.

This is not nitpicking. Each of us has a view of the whole picture; some people say it out loud and some do not. The philosopher of religion John Hick offered the strongest version of this idea: there is only one ultimate Reality, every religion is a different culture’s response to it, and every religion can change human lives. This is serious thought and must not be brushed aside. But his critics also point out that secular values can change lives too, and that changing a life does not necessarily prove everyone has met the same One.
The spiritual meaning: respect begins with understanding

Brothers and sisters, real respect is listening carefully to what the other person is actually saying, and not smoothing away their differences for them. If I say to a Muslim friend, “Actually what you believe and what I believe are the same,” he will most likely not thank me, because his scripture plainly does not accept that Jesus is the Son of God. To describe someone’s faith as the same as mine looks polite, but it is really not listening.
2. All flights have wings, but the destinations differ

You have all been to an airport. Look at the flights, the one to Tokyo, the one to Auckland, the one to Kuala Lumpur: they all have wings, all have flight attendants, all require a seat belt, and even the meals are about equally bad. They are alike, and they are all good planes. But you would never walk up to the counter and say, “Miss, they’re all the same, just give me any flight.”

Religions are like this too. Urging people to do good is a real common ground, and we thank God for it. Paul said that the Gentiles show the work of the law written in their hearts, “their conscience testifying with them.” God has put a conscience in every person. So your grandma who goes to the temple is very kind, and that is true.

But ask deeper: what is humanity’s greatest problem? Where is the way out? The answers differ. Buddhism says the problem of life is suffering, which comes from attachment, and the way out is the cessation of attachment. The Hindu tradition is extremely diverse, and many in it seek release from the cycle of rebirth. Confucianism puts its effort into human relationships in this world, and Confucius said, “You do not yet understand life, so how can you understand death?” Daoism says to follow the Dao that cannot be clearly spoken. Islam stresses submission to the one God. I am speaking very roughly. My friends can surely add to this, and you are welcome to go and ask them yourself.

What does the Christian faith say? The human problem is a broken relationship with God. The way out is not a method but a person. God Himself became a human being, died on the cross, and rose on the third day. Other differences can be discussed slowly, but there is one thing we cannot fudge: did Jesus die on the cross or not? Most Muslims think not; Christians think so. It cannot be both yes and no.

For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, (1 Corinthians 15:3-4)

Here is the most powerful objection, and I do not want to skip it: you believe in Jesus only because you happened to be born in that setting, don’t you? Born in Thailand, you would most likely be Buddhist; born in Saudi Arabia, most likely Muslim. There is something to this. Culture’s influence on faith is real, and we must honestly admit it. Still, where an idea comes from and whether it is true are two different things. Otherwise the idea that “all religions are the same” has its birthplace too.
So why does God let people be born in different places? Honestly, I do not have a complete answer to this question, and it grieves me too. In the next unit we will come back to face it.
The spiritual meaning: He came down

Friends, if you ask me to state the difference of the gospel in one sentence, I would put it this way: many roads teach people how to go up, and the gospel tells how God came down. Paul says He “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” all the way down, “yes, the death of the cross.” If a person tries to climb up to heaven, however high he climbs, there will always be someone higher, and always someone who cannot climb. God came down, and the one who can least climb is the first to be able to touch Him.
3. How do we say “only” without arrogance?

But Jesus’ words are very direct: “No one comes to the Father, except through me.” Peter also said: “There is salvation in no one else.” To our ears today this does not sound very polite. Please notice that when Peter said this, he was standing on trial before the rulers. The sentence did not bring him power. It brought him trouble.

Now look at what Paul did. When he arrived in Athens, the whole city was full of idols, and he was deeply troubled. But he did not smash the altars. He first walked around and looked carefully, and then said, “I perceive that you are very religious in all things.” He saw an altar inscribed “TO AN UNKNOWN GOD,” and began from there. He even quoted their poets. Only then did he say plainly that Jesus had risen from the dead. Clear, and courteous.

He made from one blood every nation of men to dwell on all the surface of the earth, having determined appointed seasons and the boundaries of their dwellings, that they should seek the Lord, if perhaps they might reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from each one of us. (Acts 17:26-27)

A pastor from Sri Lanka named D. T. Niles wrote in his 1951 book that evangelism is one beggar telling another beggar where to find food. On the internet it is often changed to “bread,” but the original is food.

I love this saying. A beggar who finds food does not become a higher class of person because of it. He was only hungry, he ate, and he knows you are hungry too, so he comes running to tell you. When he tells you, he does not put his feet up.

We must also admit that in the history of the church, some people oppressed others in the name of Christ. Christians often do not look like Christ. When we face such an accusation, we need not hurry to defend ourselves; where an apology is due, we apologize. When two of Jesus’ disciples wanted to command fire to come down from the sky and destroy a village that would not receive them, Jesus rebuked them.
The spiritual meaning: letting God be God

Our responsibility is to point the way clearly and bring people to Jesus. How each heart stands, only God can see through. Let God be God and let people be people. We often speak of the self-centered and the selfless: the self-centered person shares the gospel to prove himself right, and the selfless person shares the gospel because he himself is loved, and loves the person in front of him.

So the next time the elder pinches a piece of chicken and asks you, you can smile and say, “You’re right. Every religion urges people toward goodness, and that is very beautiful. But I have also found that they actually give quite different answers to life’s questions. I believe in Jesus because I found I could not do it on my own, and He came down to find me. If you are interested, I would love to share with you. If not, that’s fine too. Let me put some chicken on your plate.”

This week, please do one thing: ask a friend of a different faith, “What matters most to you in your faith?” Listen quietly to the end, do not argue, and thank them sincerely. When you have understood first, your words will carry weight later.
Let us be quiet for a moment and think of a relative or friend whom we respect but whose faith differs from ours, and thank God for that person’s goodness.

Let us pray together. Lord Jesus, You are the way, the truth and the life. Thank You for not waiting for me to climb up, but coming down Yourself to find me. Remove the pride in my heart, so that I dare to speak the truth and also have a gentle heart. Let the friends around me with different faiths see Your kindness in me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
