2. What impact does the objection “you believe what you were born into” have on you? How did you yourself come to the faith you hold today?
3. Which friend of a different faith around you could you go and ask first, and listen to first? How do you plan to start the conversation?
Can Good People Go to Heaven?
for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast. (Ephesians 2:8-9)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Pastors attend many funerals, and the sentence we hear most is this: “He was a good man.” “Such a good person must have gone to heaven.” The people who say this have red eyes, and you really cannot bear to ask anything more.

Today’s topic is very hard to speak about: can good people go to heaven? Let me lay my cards on the table. First, I want to say honestly that some friends who do not believe in Jesus are kinder than many Christians, including me. Second, someone here today has come with a very painful question: my grandfather and grandmother, my father and mother, never heard of Jesus until they died. What happens to them? I will not dodge this question, but I will not pretend to know what I do not know.
1. The report card of a good person

Let me ask you: do you count as a good person? Most people will say, “I think so. I haven’t murdered or set fires. I’m a lot better than so-and-so.” You see, when we grade ourselves, there always has to be a so-and-so standing next to us. It is like when you were little and got a sixty on a test, and you went home and told your mother, “Ah-Ming next door only got a forty.” I tried that trick. It did not work.

Jesus told a parable about two men who went up to the temple to pray. Do not picture that Pharisee as a villain. He was truly the model student of his day. He fasted twice a week, and gave a tenth of all his income, and in any church today he could be an elder. The other was a tax collector who collected taxes for the Romans, and everyone looked down on him.
But the tax collector, standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his chest, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’ (Luke 18:13)

Jesus said that the one who went home justified was this man. The listeners of that day must have been stunned. Jesus was not saying that the Pharisee’s fasting and giving were bad. He was looking at whom that man was comparing himself with in his heart, and what he was relying on.

Some will also say: I only make little mistakes once in a while. Does God really keep such strict accounts? James says: “For whoever keeps the whole law, and yet stumbles in one point, he has become guilty of all.” At first this sounds very harsh, but think of a glass. Once a crack runs through it, it can no longer be called an unbroken glass, and how many cracks there are is only a matter of degree. As for the standard between a person and God, Jesus’ own words are: “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.” If you are starting to break into a cold sweat, congratulations: you have reached the door of the gospel.
The son who had not gone home in twenty years

Let me paint a picture. There is a son who is good to the whole village. He repairs the roads, donates schools, and when an elderly person is sick, he is the first to arrive. The whole village says what a good child he is. But there is one thing no one knows: for twenty years he has not gone home to see his father. When his father phones, he does not answer, and he does not even want to mention his father’s name. Friends, we Chinese understand this at once. However well you treat your neighbors, the account cannot be settled this way, can it?

The sin of which the Bible speaks begins right here. Jesus said the greatest commandment is to love God with all your heart, and the second is to love your neighbor as yourself. The scores we give each other almost only look at the second, and even on the second we do not necessarily pass. Paul says that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. This is not saying that everyone is a villain. It is saying that everyone has left home.
The spiritual meaning: goodness is real, but goodness cannot repair a relationship

Christians should not deny other people’s goodness. That looks ugly and is not honest. The Bible says that people have a sense of right and wrong engraved in their hearts by God, and those good deeds are gifts from God. But we must also say gently that good deeds cannot repair that broken relationship between father and son. The repair requires the father to reach out first.
A road that runs the other way

The methods of self-cultivation around the world are all rather like mountain climbing, teaching people to become better step by step, and these all deserve respect. The Christian faith says something very strange: people cannot finish climbing this mountain, so the One at the top came down Himself. He came down to Bethlehem, and down to Golgotha. This is today’s key verse: “For by grace you have been saved through faith.”

I explain this word grace through adoption. In this world no child is adopted because of a report card, and no child trades a certificate of merit for a father and mother. But after a child is adopted, he slowly comes to have the ways of his father and mother. Good deeds come the same way. They are the fruit and not the root. That is why Ephesians says in the very next verse, verse ten: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works.” There is a passage in Matthew 25 that moves me every time I read it. The King says to the righteous that they did well, and they actually ask back, “Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you…?” They were not keeping accounts at all! True grace makes people forget even that they did good.

The scene in the whole Bible that speaks most about grace happened at Golgotha. Hanging next to Jesus was a robber. The Bible does not mention that he was ever baptized or ever gave an offering. His hands and feet were nailed, and he did not even have the chance to turn over a new leaf or do one good deed. He said only one sentence:
He said to Jesus, “Lord, remember me when you come into your Kingdom.” Jesus said to him, “Assuredly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise.” (Luke 23:42-43)

You may ask, is that fair? A man who did evil all his life has his last sentence count, and what about the kind old person? We must listen seriously to this question. The cross tells us that evil was not simply erased: the price was paid with Jesus’ life. Notice also that this robber first admitted he deserved what he got. Grace is not cheap. It is only that someone else pays.
The spiritual meaning: you can stop comparing

What is the greatest release of grace? You can stop comparing. You no longer have to compare yourself with so-and-so, and no longer have to count at three in the morning whether your merits are enough. For us Chinese, who have been compared since we were small, this is truly the best news in the world.
Evangelicals do not have one answer either

We come now to the most painful question. Let me tell you honestly: the Bible does not set this out as clearly as a timetable, and even godly theologians who love the Lord hold different views. Some hold that a person must hear and believe in this life, citing Romans 10: “How will they believe in him whom they have not heard?” The Lausanne Movement’s Manila Manifesto of 1989 leans in this direction. Others hold that people can be saved only through Christ, yet some who have never heard His name may respond to the light God has given them and be saved through Christ. A few think there may be a chance after death, though the scriptural basis for that camp is harder. The British pastor John Stott, a much respected leader among evangelicals, said that God has not revealed how He will treat those who have never heard, and he preferred to leave the question open. C. S. Lewis in Mere Christianity has a similar humility. I will not rule on this for you here. Your own church may have its own teaching, so please talk it over carefully with your pastor.

Someone will ask again: does where you are born decide everything? Paul in Athens said that God has “determined appointed seasons and the boundaries of their dwellings, that they should seek the Lord,” and that “he is not far from each one of us.” Jesus also said, “To whomever much is given, of him will much be required.” Those who did not know and those who knew are not measured by God with the same ruler. Stott held a hope that the number of the saved would be as large as Revelation describes, “a great multitude which no man could count.” This is his personal hope, not a promise of the Bible, but it is a hope well worth keeping in our hearts.
The verse we can stand on

So what can we be sure of? First, salvation is only through Christ, and there is no second name. Second, the One who judges is perfectly fair. When Abraham interceded for Sodom he said something I would like the brothers and sisters who have tears in their eyes to write down:
Shouldn’t the Judge of all the earth do right? (Genesis 18:25)

He loves your grandfather and grandmother more than you do. He knows all their struggles in life, whether they had a chance, and what they cried out to heaven. I cannot tell you where they are, and no one can, including the one who sounds so certain in front of you. I can only tell you whose hands they are in. Please entrust them to Him.

A word about ancestor rites. Quite a few people worry that believing in Jesus means being unfilial. The fifth commandment says in black and white to honor your father and mother, and a Christian should be more filial than anyone. As for what to do at Qingming, the tomb-sweeping festival, churches have different practices. Many use a memorial service, with thanksgiving, flowers and stories about the ancestors, and some theologians have proposed more detailed approaches. My advice is: do not pray to the dead, but arrive earlier than anyone, be better at sweeping the grave, and show more respect to the elders. That witness is far more useful than debate.
The spiritual meaning: entrust judgment to God, and give love to the living

There is something we can do, and can do today: there are still people alive. You may not know the final destiny of a relative who has died, but you know that your father and mother can still pick up the phone today. Do not use threats. Jesus came not “to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him.” He did speak seriously of an eternal separation. We do not turn this into a tool for frightening people. We invite with tears and with love.

The heaven we speak of is not a warehouse of prizes. It is a home. Revelation says that God will dwell with people and Himself wipe away every tear. This home is not a ticket bought with grades; it was paid in full by the firstborn Son with His life. Of our three foundations, the Bible is my standard, so we follow the Bible: what should be affirmed, we affirm, and what should be entrusted, we entrust. Of our two cores, Let Jesus reign means that we hand even the seat of who gets into heaven back to Him. This is letting God be God and letting people be people.

If today you find that you have been living on “I’m a good person,” you are welcome to switch to another prayer. That prayer is very short, just one sentence: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” Jesus said that the one who prays like this goes home justified.
Let us be quiet. Think of the name you are carrying. Think of yourself too.

Let us pray together. Heavenly Father, I lay down my report card. I need Your grace; be merciful to me, a sinner. Thank You, Lord Jesus, for paying the price for me. I place my relatives who have died into Your hands. You are just and loving, and I trust You. Give me courage and gentleness to bring this love to the family members who are still living. In Jesus’ name, amen.

How to Begin Walking with God
that if you will confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. (Romans 10:9)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Today is the last exhibit hall in Life’s Questions Hall, and the final stop of the whole app. If you have come all the way through, you have seen the galaxies, you have seen the cell, and you have seen human history and the most painful questions in the human heart. Today we will not look at one more exhibit. Today we ask one question: and then what?

Let me set the ground rules first. When I finish speaking today, I will not ask you to raise your hand, I will not play moving music, and no one will be pushing you from behind. If faith is something you are pushed into, it walks out the door as soon as you do. Today I will do only one thing: make things clear, and open the door. Whether to walk in is between you and God.
The Bible has a beautiful line: “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart.” The universe is so vast, and yet this distance is so short. We will walk it in three parts.
1. God speaks first: you are loved, and you have wandered off
He loves you, not your résumé
The most famous verse in the whole Bible, which many people have heard even if they have never read the Bible:
For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. (John 3:16)

Notice the two words “the world.” You are in it. The you who came first in the exam is in it, and so is the you who feels you have accomplished nothing. In Chinese society, a lot of people grew up hearing love with conditions attached: we love you if you test well, we love you if you make us proud, we acknowledge you if you earn money. God’s love is different. He reaches out before you have performed anything.

The second sentence is harder to hear, but a doctor who will not tell you the diagnosis is not a good doctor either. “All have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God.” Earlier we said that sin is not only breaking a law; sin is leaving home. We put ourselves in the middle, hold the steering wheel ourselves, and treat God as a number to call in an emergency. The Bible says the result of going on like this is very serious:
For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. (Romans 6:23)

Doesn’t this verse look like a statement of account? The first half is what you earn, called wages. The second half is what someone else gives, called a gift. What you earn through a lifetime of hard work is death; what you receive for free is life. This verse really does not fit our work ethic.

Jesus told a story that we all know well. The younger son spent all the family property, ended up fighting with pigs for food, and finally decided to go home. On the road he kept rehearsing his lines: how to open his mouth, how to confess his wrong. And what happened?
He arose and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him. (Luke 15:20)

“While he was still far off.” That father must have been looking down the road every day to recognize his child from so far away. Friends, however far you have walked, there is someone waiting for you at the other end of this road.
The spiritual meaning: know you are loved first, and then you dare to face sin

Please notice the order. Without the first sentence, the second would crush a person. Without the second sentence, the first would become sweet talk. A child who is sure his father loves him dares to bring out the broken vase and admit it. If today you want to run away when you think of your sin, please go back to the first sentence: He loves you.
2. God came Himself: He died, and He lives
But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. (Romans 5:8)

The key word in this verse is “yet.” While we were yet sinners. Not after we cleaned ourselves up, not after we quit something, and not after we learned to pray. Think about it: “one will hardly die for a righteous man,” and Christ died for a people who were still against Him and had not yet thanked Him. That price, He paid Himself.

If the story ended there, we would have a great and pitiable martyr. The Bible goes on to say that on the third day He rose. When the apostle Paul wrote to the Corinthians, he said this was what he passed on “first of all,” “that which I also received.” Scholars have found that this passage is itself an earlier tradition, and scholars’ estimates average about five years after Jesus’ death for it to have taken shape. That does not mean history makes the decision of faith for you. We discussed the evidence for the resurrection in Jesus Hall, and friends who have not yet seen it can go back and look. But you should know that the earliest core of the Christian faith is this one thing: He died, and He lives.
The spiritual meaning: the gospel is news that has already happened

Most teachings tell you what you “should do.” The gospel first tells you what “has already happened.” That is why it is called gospel, good news. You did not come to receive a longer to-do list. You came to hear a report: the price is paid, the tomb is empty, the door is open.
3. Your turn: turn around, and entrust yourself
The shortest answer in the Bible

In Acts 16 there is a jailer. In the middle of the night an earthquake opened every prison door, and thinking the prisoners had escaped, he was about to take his own life. Paul shouted to stop him. This man, trembling all over, asked the most important question in the world: “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” Their answer was strikingly short: “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household.” They did not tell him to go study for three years first, or to quit his job first. It simply began like that. So what is believing? I will explain with two actions.

Many people hear the word repentance and think it means weeping and wailing. Tears may come or may not. Repentance means the direction changes. I was driving this way, I found I was going the wrong way, and I make a U-turn. Change your mindset, then change your life, then change how you live: that is the order. You do not need to get your life in order before you come. You would not wash yourself clean before taking a bath, would you?

Believing is not only the head agreeing either. You can study the material of a chair, its structure and its load capacity, and write a report concluding that the chair should hold. But only when you actually sit down and give your whole weight to it do you believe in the chair. Romans 10 says, “with the heart one believes resulting in righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made resulting in salvation”: one inside, one outside. Put your weight on Jesus, and then say it out loud.

I often hear a few things. Some say, “I’m not good enough yet. I’ll come after I get rid of my bad habits.” But that is like waiting until you are well to see a doctor. Some say, “I still have many questions I can’t figure out.” You may come with your questions; the disciples followed Jesus for three years and were still asking. Some say, “If I believe, will I become unfilial?” Be assured, the Bible tells us to honor our father and mother, and you will only learn how to love them better.

I also have to be honest about the cost. Jesus said that anyone who builds a tower should first sit down and count the cost. Following Him does not guarantee you wealth, does not guarantee that illness will be healed, and in some families there will be pressure. If in your situation believing could bring conflict, or even legal risk, please be careful, first talk with a pastor you trust, and there is no need to rush to go public. The promise He gives is that He is with you, and that “He who comes to me I will in no way throw out.”
The spiritual meaning: this step is a starting line, not a graduation ceremony

A decision is not like getting an insurance policy and going home. It is more like the day of a wedding: the wedding matters, but your days together are only beginning. At the same time, do not go the other way and be afraid, thinking you must be sure you can walk for a lifetime before you dare to begin. “He who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.” The strength to keep walking is also given by Him.
If you are not ready today

This is what I most want to say to you: that’s all right. If you still have questions, if you are still thinking, that is all right. God is not a department store anniversary sale; the offer does not end after today. There was a father who brought his child to Jesus, and he said, “I believe. Help my unbelief!” Jesus did not send him away. Today you can pray a very honest prayer: “God, if You are really there, let me come to know You.” Jesus said, “Seek, and you will find.” This is a real beginning.

There are a few simple steps from here. First, tell a Christian, today or tomorrow. If you do not know anyone, you are welcome to find us on the YouTube channel of Kingdom 321 Air Fellowship; the account is kingdom321air. Second, read a little Bible every day, starting with the Gospel of John, one chapter a day. Third, talk with God every day, as you would talk with your dad. Fourth, find a spiritual family, a church that takes the Bible as its standard and Christ as its center. The Air Fellowship can be a bridge, but if there is a healthy church near your home, we also encourage you to walk into it, because people need an embrace they can see. A healthy church does not control you, and does not pressure you for money. If you live overseas, or cannot find a church nearby for now, do not give up because of that; begin online, and ask God to lead you to people who will walk with you. Fifth, when the time comes, talk with a pastor about baptism. And after that? Every relationship, every day, is your training ground: lay yourself down and bear the fruit of the Spirit. Let Jesus reign, and let Jesus receive all the glory. Walk on like this, and you will become an overcomer too.

One more reminder: when you wake up tomorrow morning, you may not feel anything special. The same alarm clock, the same boss, the same pile of bills. This is normal. Your salvation does not depend on feelings; it depends on His promise. First John says: “These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life.” It says know, not guess. Feelings change like the weather, but the promise does not change.
Now please be quiet. No one is watching you. If the prayer below is the words of your heart, you can pray along with me. If it is not, you can simply listen.

Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for loving me. I admit that I am a sinner. I have been living my own way and have left You. Please forgive me. I believe that Jesus Christ is Your Son, that He died on the cross for my sins and rose from the dead on the third day. Today I am willing to turn to You and receive Jesus as my Savior and the Lord of my life. Holy Spirit, come into my heart and help me follow You every day. In Jesus’ name, amen.
If you prayed this prayer just now, the Bible says that “there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.” Welcome home. Do not walk alone; tell one person today.
